With their flagship morning shows on Wednesday, ABC and CBS continued the liberal, elitist media-wide campaign to take as certified, unavoidable truth the claims from certain corners of the artificial intelligence (AI) sector that AI will not only take over the planet, but “poses a threat to humanity” that’ll leave billions of people dead.
That mindset was evident as ABC’s Good Morning America and CBS Mornings melted down over Tuesday’s White House AI summit, which concluded without an announcement of sweeping, iron-fisted government regulations to assume control of the industry.
ABC was, as usual, the most hyperbolic. Co-host and former Clinton official George Stephanopoulos screeched that Trump “downplay[ed] the risks of AI, saying at a lunch with tech executives that the companies can police themselves despite warnings that AI poses a threat to humanity.”
ABC’s ‘Good Morning America’ was particularly unhinged when it came to melting down over Trump’s AI summit.
George Stephanopoulos screeched the President “downplay[ed] the risks of AI, saying...companies can police themselves despite warnings that AI poses a threat to humanity.”… pic.twitter.com/qDR01fshQg
Senior political correspondent and virulent Trump hater Rachel Scott relayed that the President “insists that there’s no need for the federal government to step in and rein in this technology, instead leaving it up to the companies to regulate themselves,” even though “the very tech leaders” he saw “have sounded the alarm about AI.” 
Scott doubled down on the apocalyptic scenarios: “With the most powerful tech executives standing behind him, President Trump declaring AI leaders should police themselves after weeks of dire warnings about the threat it could pose to humanity.”
She scoffed at the signed joint agreement, whining “[t]here will be no federal guardrails on AI,” and that Tuesday’s lunch instead resulted in “a voluntary joint agreement.”
Moments later, she contrasted Trump with the side she herself finds reasonable versus Trump, who has “dismissed those concerns, rejecting calls to regulate AI as a globalist scheme”:
She contrasted Trump with the side she herself finds reasonable, playing up clips of Dario Amodei arguing his company could be dangerous and Bill Gates predicting AI could murder billions of people pic.twitter.com/mrWRdQFDrR
— Curtis Houck (@CurtisHouck) September 30, 2026
She concluded by showing herself founding Trump and pointing to a Quinnipiac University poll backing up her argument the government needs to, in essence, assume control of the industry (click “expand”):

— Curtis Houck (@CurtisHouck) September 30, 2026

TRUMP: It’s not a hoax. It’s a very serious. That’s why I changed the name.
SCOTT: Okay.

So again, this agreement is voluntary. It’s legally non-binding. It also comes as a new poll from Quinnipiac University shows that 79 percent of voters would rather have safety when it comes to AI instead of advancements in this technology.
Over at CBS Mornings, they showed that, yet again, it’s not the MAGA TV that the media reporting class has insisted.
Co-host Nate Burleson panned the summit: “A White House meeting on the potential dangers of AI left many people wondering just how much was achieved. The tech CEOs who met with President Trump did agree on a request to police themselves, but critics say much stronger guardrails are needed.”
Senior White House and political correspondent Ed O’Keefe said the “extraordinary” and “unprecedented gathering” featured “titans of the world’s fastest-growing and potentially most dangerous industry” who signed onto “a new set of voluntary safety standards.”
“But Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who raised the loudest concerns about the dangers of AI and wants more government intervention, expressed caution...The President and Speaker dismissed more government regulation of the AI industry, but Democrats are pushing for more action to ensure safety,” he later added.
Unlike ABC, CBS and O’Keefe brought up Trump’s comments about building data centers:
The President also said he discussed the construction of data centers with the AI leaders, saying he still wants them built in the U.S., but away from homes. He suggested building them could provide more economic incentives in communities where they’re being built, such as dividends to residents or bonuses for local schoolteachers.
Over on NBC’s Today, co-host Craig Melvin said “the growing debate and concern surrounding AI” led to “that historic White House summit between President Trump and some of the nation’s leading tech titans.”
Senior White House correspondent Gabe Gutierrez emphasized right off the bat that “there are growing questions about how binding [the] agreement really is” between Trump and “some of those powerful business leaders in the world, leading companies worth trillions of dollars.”
“This morning, after an extraordinary meeting at the White House, the U.S.’s biggest tech giants are now attempting to go present a united front, despite sharp disagreements over whether AI needs more guardrails...President Trump rejecting calls for more government regulation, instead releasing a signed document,” he said.

sources.news_title: Trump’s AI Safety ‘Accord’ Is a Fancy Pinky-Swear
sources.text:
On Tuesday, executives for Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and Nvidia all signed “The White House Accord on Super Intelligence,” which was announced following a luncheon held by President Donald Trump.
The effort was an act of “tremendous self-regulation,” as Trump put it, but the agreement is not the sweeping AI regulation that people inside the companies themselves have been asking for. And while failing to honor these public commitments could count as illegally lying to consumers, even that wouldn’t be enough to trigger massive reforms.
The statement says that companies “should implement” several things: First, they should ensure they have “robust internal controls” to monitor their models’ capabilities and ability to not go rogue or hack things in unintended ways. Second, they should “empower” an internal team to do that work (and remediate when things go wrong). Third, it encourages them to partner with an external monitor who is “empowered” to do independent assessments to make sure that all of that work is happening. And finally, they should make sure their board of directors has set up a committee to receive reports about all of these efforts.
The voluntary commitments are some indication that the frontier labs are making an effort to figure out how to make products that are safe for the general public. However, if there were any hopes for a blanket blessing from the US government, those were quickly dashed after news broke that the Federal Trade Commission intends to investigate several AI companies over potential consumer protection issues.
The statement is the culmination of weeks of debate over AI regulation. It also follows frontier AI labs seeking an antitrust exemption so they can coordinate on safety work without regulatory scrutiny. (Notably, antitrust experts and practitioners say such an exemption is unneeded because AI ending humanity—which researchers have warned will come about if nothing is done—is arguably anti-competitive because humans are an essential part of any given marketplace.)
There’s been a lot of build-up to this particular statement, but this is not the first time that these companies have signed a voluntary agreement about their AI safety practices with a government. In early 2025, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Korea announced a set of “Frontier AI Safety Commitments,” which included promises about doing internal and external red-teaming of AI models for “severe and novel threats” and also “to work toward information sharing” on AI safety issues.
Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment. The White House also did not immediately respond.
Neil Chilson, a former chief technologist for the FTC, posted on X of the accords that “this is the kind of pledge that the FTC could potentially enforce, if a company materially failed to follow through on any of these promises.”
But those hoping for a sweeping settlement and a dramatic reining-in of rogue “super intelligence” based on the accords alone might find themselves disappointed.
(Disclosure: This story’s author previously worked in the Office of Technology at the FTC and resigned in November 2025.)
Not following through on a public promise could be considered a deceptive business practice and a violation of the FTC Act. When the FTC alleges that a company deceived its customers, the remedy it usually prescribes is making the company promise not to lie again.
For example, the FTC recently announced it had settled with three companies after it alleged they were touting a service that could help businesses target ads based on audio recordings collected from smartphones, smart TVs, and other devices. The companies, the agency said, lied to businesses about their ability to creep on consumers. The fix? The companies are no longer allowed to misrepresent their advertising services and the collection and use of consumers’ voice data, among other things. The case does not address whether it’s OK to collect voice data from your phone, and the settlement doesn’t set out any guardrails if one of the three companies wanted to actually do that in the future (other than not lying about it.)
OpenAI has been remarkably open about the number of times its agents have broken into other people’s systems and how it needs to improve its safety practices. But, as experts have pointed out to WIRED, the US government can open investigations into companies even if they eventually decide there’s no enforcement action to bring. (The FTC, for example, reportedly sent a civil investigative demand to OpenAI in 2023, but it’s unclear what came of that.)
Following Tuesday’s AI luncheon with Trump, the New York Post reported that the FTC was planning a “sweeping probe” into Anthropic, OpenAI, other unnamed frontier labs, and a nonprofit called METR that does third-party evaluations. METR and the labs didn’t respond to a request for comment.
The Post says that the agency still hasn’t issued any civil investigative demands to its intended targets—usually one of the first steps in any sort of investigation. An FTC spokesperson confirmed that there is some sort of investigation, but they declined to provide any additional details, including what consumer protection issues were of concern.
FTC chairman Andrew Ferguson, who was included on the “super intelligence” luncheon’s seating chart, has previously explained that enforcers don’t always have a fully baked case from the get-go. “You're constantly looking for smoke to see if there's fire,” he told a crowd of antitrust enthusiasts last year.
Even if the FTC investigation moves forward and the agency does identify violations, some are skeptical that it will result in any action against the AI firms.
“It should be encouraging to Americans worried about AI that the FTC is investigating these companies,” says Douglas Farrar, who was the head of public affairs for the FTC during Lina Khan’s tenure as chair. “But let’s remember that Ferguson may chair the FTC, but Donald Trump runs it, and I doubt after yesterday's love fest with his AI CEO buddies that Trump will allow any legal action with teeth against these companies.”

sources.news_title: Trump's 'AI Accord' Does Little to Actually Keep AI Safe, Experts Say
sources.text:
Leaders from major tech companies met at the White House on Tuesday to discuss what’s been on everyone’s mind this summer: AI safety. Afterward, President Donald Trump announced that the group had reached a consensus to implement AI safety measures in a voluntary accord.
The accord, which Trump posted on Truth Social, outlines four main layers of controls that AI companies should implement. It also misspells United as “Unites” in Trump’s title under his signature.
- “Implement robust internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models during training and deployment” for areas of grave concern, like cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats
- Create and empower an internal team dedicated to ensuring safety issues are identified and fixed
- “Partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator” to ensure safety protocols are working as intended
- Create an independent committee of the company’s board of directors to oversee and receive reports from internal safety teams, independent auditors and evaluators
Signees are a “who’s who” of Big Tech, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI President Greg Brockman. (OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was delivering the opening keynote of OpenAI’s DevDay in San Francisco on Tuesday.)
More from CNET
It’s a ceremonial move, as is Trump’s new executive order to refer to AI as “super intelligence.” Trump told reporters on Tuesday that the accord is “morally binding” rather than legally mandatory. It doesn’t have the power of law or any way to enforce it.
Big tech companies are already self-policing, Trump said. The Trump administration has taken a hands-off approach to regulating AI, with a few exceptions when the White House identified certain AI tools as a threat to national security.
Most executive action on AI has been purely discretionary — from the Biden administration’s AI safety pledge to Trump’s ratepayer protection pledge to address data center-driven increases in utility bills. While many big tech companies have agreed in theory, their emphasis on growth and investor cash flow downplays concerns about the environment, rising consumer costs and safety.
“When you look at this particular accord, I think these are amazing general steps that we should be moving toward,” said John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, a cybersecurity firm. “The thing that bothers me is that there’s no implementation or monitoring mechanism to make sure these organizations actually adhere to the standards they say they’re going to follow.”
Self-regulation in the tech industry has already proven ineffective. AI companies have struggled to control their own models, leading to instances where bots escaped their training environments and hacked government websites in both the US and Australia. Despite warnings that they are unprepared for a catastrophic “AI doomsday” scenario — and public discussions over slowdowns or pauses in AI development — labs plow ahead with new tools.
That’s why Anthony Aguirre, CEO of the Future of Life Institute, a nonprofit focused on reducing risks of advanced tech, argues that we can’t trust tech companies to police themselves.
“These companies have jettisoned safety commitments countless times before, and they will do so again. Self-regulation is what has gotten us teen suicides, 1,200 rogue AI bots and an international cybercrime spree. The risk of inaction — both politically and morally — is massive,” Aguirre said.
Beyond the weak ability to enforce the accord, there are other potential pitfalls. One is the notion of an “independent” auditor or evaluator, which may not be so clear-cut. AI engineers and executives are notorious for jumping around from lab to lab — Apple even sued OpenAI for violating its trade secrets.
In a close-knit field like AI, it’s not impossible for those subcontractors to be friends and business partners of the AI companies they would monitor, Gary Marcus, an AI expert and professor emeritus at New York University, wrote in a recent Substack post.
“Its weak point is the word independent,” said Jacob Krell, senior director at Suzu Labs, a cybersecurity and AI firm. “Layer three lets each company choose an external evaluator but says nothing about accreditation, method, access, scope, or publication.”
That kind of transparency and documentation matter a lot for cybersecurity defenders working to keep their customers’ sites secure from rogue or intentional AI agent hacks.
Although the new agreement suggests eventually turning these AI guidelines into formal laws, Congress hasn’t reached consensus on how it wants to regulate the technology.
Rep. Ro Khanna, a Democrat who represents Silicon Valley, criticized the voluntary agreement in an X post, “We are a nation of laws, not pinky promises.” Khanna recently introduced a new bill that would impose limits on recursive self-improvement, alongside other pending legislation, such as Sen. Bernie Sanders’ bill to ban superintelligence.
Meanwhile, the Federal Trade Commission opened an inquiry into major AI labs — including Anthropic and OpenAI — to investigate the risks their AI agents and technology pose to consumers, according to multiple reports.

sources.news_title: Trump and six tech companies sign a voluntary artificial intelligence safety accord
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump and the heads of six technology companies signed a voluntary accord at the White House on Tuesday under which the companies commit to ensuring the safety of their own artificial intelligence systems. Trump called it “morally binding” and said it was “almost like a constitution”.
The document, titled “White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities”, was posted by the president on his Truth Social network after a lunch with industry executives. It was signed by Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Jensen Huang of Nvidia and Elon Musk.
According to the text, the companies are responsible for the safety of their own technology, will implement safeguards so models operate as intended, will quickly detect and fix problems and will work with independent auditors to verify their systems do not access other technical systems in unintended ways. The accord sets no consequences for breaches. Trump also announced a board to oversee the area, without naming its members, and the appointment of a government official to lead on the issue in the coming days.
Zuckerberg described it as “a start”; Pichai as “historic and consequential”; and Amodei as a way “to win safely”. Specialists consulted by the BBC were critical. Kimberlee Weatherall, a law professor at the University of Sydney, said the accord lets companies “define what counts as safety” and called it “deeply unimpressive”. Jeannie Paterson of the University of Melbourne warned that self-regulation could mean “only minimal safeguards”.
The accord comes amid calls from parts of the industry and from experts for tighter oversight of the technology. According to the BBC, OpenAI cancelled the release of one of its models on Monday over safety concerns.
The same day, Trump signed an executive order requiring federal agencies to replace “artificial intelligence” with “Super Intelligence” or “SI” in official correspondence, websites and reports, and tasking his science and technology adviser with proposing a legal definition within 60 days. In his address to the UN General Assembly last week, the president said the word “artificial” made the technology “sound fake”.
Trump reiterated his support for the expansion of data centres, whose construction has become a sensitive issue ahead of November's midterm elections: a Marist poll for NPR and PBS found 65% of registered voters oppose having them built in their area.
The accord puts into practice the position Washington set out in New York against calls for common rules. There, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for “a single set of global principles and standards”, while Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei rejected any pre-emptive regulation.

sources.news_title: Trump plan to combat AI risks hinges on Big Tech pals policing themselves
sources.text:
Amid escalating AI security incidents causing OpenAI to halt training and pause releases, Donald Trump continues to advocate for the AI industry to regulate itself as the best path to combat emerging risks when developing frontier AI.
In an agreement Tuesday, two dozen tech firms voluntarily committed to implementing controls recommended by the White House, including undergoing independent safety audits that will test whether firms’ internal controls, monitoring, and detecting are actually working. Key focuses for external reviews included “risks related to cybersecurity, biosecurity, chemical threats, and unintended actions by AI models.”
Firms also agreed to regularly meet to discuss best practices and set common AI safety standards and benchmarks. Among signers were leaders like Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Alphabet/Google’s Sundar Pichai.
Nothing new is legally required of firms, and some—like Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI—had already committed to external audits, The Information reported. Additionally, many firms have voluntarily committed to highly secretive government safety testing. Adding to these tests, Trump insisted the Tuesday deal will somehow better address real emerging risks and is “morally binding,” despite carrying no legal weight, Bloomberg reported.
“It’s almost like a constitution, in a way,” Trump told reporters at the White House following a lunch with tech leaders. “The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection.”
Eventually, it “may make sense to codify” the recommendations, the agreement said near the end. But for now, Trump stressed that the best possible future for the US requires trusting AI firms to regulate themselves.
Trump’s Big Tech friends embrace “SI”
So far, very few details have been released about how the new round of safety audits would work. Trump has only posted a summary of the accord on Truth Social.
It’s also unclear who Trump is tapping to audit frontier models. Bloomberg noted that Trump seems to be politicizing the selection process, while some AI firms appear uncertain what might qualify as a third party to test their frontier AI. Some progress has been made already in finding candidates, though, as Bloomberg reported that “some of the firms poised to conduct those reviews have already met” with the US agency conducting voluntary government pre-deployment safety tests, the Center for AI Standards and Innovation.

sources.text:
On Tuesday, President Trump announced a voluntary agreement with the heads of six major AI companies to keep “superintelligence” in check. The one-page document inspired mockery from AI experts and commentators around the Internet.
The signatories to the agreement included OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk, and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.
The pledge is “morally binding,” Trump told attendees at a press conference, as if to underscore the fact that there is nothing legally binding about it. “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations,” the agreement notes in its closing remarks. As it stands, the agreement seems like little more than a handshake between an industry known for cutthroat competition and failure to self-regulate, and a government that seems antagonistic to regulation, not to mention, morality.
Read more: “AI Engineers Are Having Their Oppenheimer “Destroyer of Worlds” Moment
“Reading the accord between the lines,” wrote American psychologist Gary Marcus, a consistently vocal critic of generative artificial intelligence, on his substack, the pledge amounts to saying, “1. We agree not to be regulated. 2. We agree not to give the public a voice. 3. Trust us.”
The language of the voluntary agreement is loose. It simply allows AI firms to define safety on their own terms without outlining any consequences for breaches, said Kimberlee Weatherall, a University of Sydney law professor, in an interview with the BBC, calling the accord “deeply unimpressive.” Key terms like “alignment” and “robust internal controls” are left undefined, with no proposed way to measure them, noted Luiza Jarovsky, a global expert in AI governance, policy, and privacy regulation.
Totally absent from the document is any mention of the kind of “pacing the frontier” that the AI companies were calling for a couple of weeks ago, added Marcus on X. In mid-September—after a flurry of dire warnings about the AI apocalypse began to flood social media, set off by a post on X by Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic who quit to air his concerns—Amodei penned a treatise about the need to slow development of new models until appropriate safeguards could catch up.
Amodei also said the most effective way to do this would be to regulate all United States-based frontier AI companies, requiring both transparency and third-party auditing, while formalizing permanent, embedded evaluators. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote on X in response that he agreed and committed to embedded evaluators, and xAI founder Elon Musk posted, “Dario is right.”
The apocalyptic warnings were inspired in part by emerging reports that rogue AI agents were deceiving their human evaluators, breaking out into the Internet and doing things they weren’t authorized to do, including coordinating attacks on companies. In the weeks since, many more incidents have come to light. Top AI companies and other security researchers are now investigating thousands of problematic incidents, according to reporting in Axios.
On the same day that the White House Accord on Superintelligence was released, a legal nonprofit in California sued OpenAI over one of the most prominent attacks its AI agents coordinated against the open-source AI platform Hugging Face earlier this year. Earlier this week, OpenAI announced that it would not release its latest model GPT 6.1 Astra over safety concerns.
“We are living in a split screen reality,” Marcus wrote. “On the left, Trump, Jensen [Huang], etc saying trust us. On the right, daily breaking news about why we absolutely should not trust OpenAI. Future generations will hate us.”
As AI safety advocate Jeff Ladish puts it on X, “Self-regulation isn’t working.”
On Tuesday, Trump also issued an executive order to announce that going forward the White House will use the term “superintelligence” to replace “artificial intelligence” in all communications. In the field of AI research, superintelligence has come to mean an AI that exceeds human intelligence in every dimension, which most experts say has not happened yet, though we are close. The term was popularized by Swedish philosopher Nick Bostrom in his 2014 book Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies.
Many experts, including computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, one of the so-called fathers of AI, have warned that once AI reaches superintelligence, humans will likely lose permanent control of it and be unable to prevent bots from pursuing goals that conflict with human interests, including resisting shut down, and potentially causing the extinction of the human race.

sources.text:
- Trump has secured a voluntary AI safety deal with Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia.
- The “morally binding” agreement does not have the force of federal law or impose new penalties.
- The deal calls for stronger AI safeguards, independent audits and board-level oversight.
US President Donald Trump has secured a voluntary commitment from leading artificial intelligence companies to police their own systems, offering a White House-backed alternative to immediate government regulation as concerns grow over increasingly autonomous AI.
Executives from Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia signed the accord after meeting Trump at the White House on Tuesday. Trump described it as “morally binding” and said the companies understood they needed to “self-police”. But the agreement does not have the force of federal law and does not set out penalties for companies that fail to meet its commitments.
Instead, the one-page accord asks companies to strengthen internal safeguards, use independent external auditors and give their boards a role in reviewing those assessments. It also leaves open the possibility that some of the measures could eventually be written into laws or regulations.
What have the AI companies agreed to?
The agreement sets out four layers of control. Companies are asked to work with independent external auditors or evaluators, establish an independent board committee to review reports from auditors and AI-control teams, maintain internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment of AI models during training and deployment, and have an internal team check that those controls, monitoring and detection systems are working as intended.
The accord also calls for internal controls to monitor AI models during training and deployment for risks including cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats, and to ensure the models do not “hack or access technical systems in unintended ways”.
That provision matters as AI developers move towards systems capable of performing tasks with limited human intervention. AI agents can interact with software, use digital tools, write and execute code and take actions on behalf of users, creating risks beyond inaccurate answers.
The aim is to put safeguards around those capabilities while subjecting the companies developing them to additional scrutiny.
The document also leaves the door open to government action. It says that, “over time”, it may make sense to codify some of the measures into laws or regulations.
What does ‘morally binding’ actually mean?
In practical terms, “morally binding” describes a public commitment backed by political and reputational pressure rather than a legal obligation.
If Congress passes a law requiring an AI company to meet a particular safety standard, the government can enforce that requirement through the legal system and impose penalties where the law allows. The White House accord does not create that kind of enforcement mechanism.
The companies have publicly agreed to follow the principles, but the accord itself creates no new offence or financial penalty for failing to do so.
AP reported that Trump described the agreement as voluntary while saying he was seeing “tremendous self-policing” among the companies. He has argued that the US should not “stifle” AI development with regulation while maintaining its lead in the technology.
Trump also described the agreement as “almost like a constitution”, portraying it as a common framework for the companies involved. But the comparison has limits. A constitution or statute establishes a formal legal framework; this accord does not.
The companies may face political, investor and reputational pressure to comply, but those consequences are different from legal enforcement. The accord itself does not give the government new powers to fine a company or block a model for failing to meet one of its commitments.
Why has AI self-regulation become an issue now?
The agreement comes as concerns grow over AI systems that can operate with greater autonomy.
Al Jazeera reported that the accord came amid growing scrutiny of AI risks following incidents involving AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic. The companies have reported cases in which their AI agents went rogue and hacked into other companies' systems, raising questions about whether safeguards can keep pace with increasingly autonomous AI.
When an AI system can act on its own, a failure can involve a real computer system, network or piece of data.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from September 17 to 20 found that 73 per cent of respondents were concerned that AI companies had not done enough to prevent serious harm from the technology, while 55 per cent said it would be good to slow AI development.
At the same time, Trump has continued to support rapid expansion of the US AI industry. Reuters reported that the White House meeting also covered the expansion of data centres needed to develop and operate increasingly powerful AI systems. Those facilities have faced opposition in some communities because of their electricity consumption and other local effects.
Self-regulation allows Trump to address some of those concerns without immediately imposing a new federal AI regime.
What happens if self-policing is not enough?
Trump has also floated a separate 10-person board to oversee AI safety more broadly.
That proposed body should not be confused with the committees that individual companies have agreed to establish. The company committees would operate within each business and review reports from internal and external auditors. The 10-person board Trump is considering would be separate from those company-level committees, although its membership and powers have not yet been defined.
Reuters reported that Trump is considering such a board and plans to appoint a new White House official responsible for AI policy. That suggests the administration is exploring government oversight while continuing to rely on voluntary commitments from the industry.
The key question is what happens after the companies sign it.
An independent audit can identify weaknesses. A company board can review those findings. But the voluntary agreement does not establish a new government penalty if a company fails to address a problem identified by an auditor.
The accord also does not settle the wider debate over whether AI companies should ultimately face mandatory safety requirements. Instead, it leaves that possibility open by acknowledging that some of its provisions could eventually be incorporated into legislation or regulation.
For Trump, the arrangement allows him to emphasise AI safety without adopting the stricter regulatory approach he has opposed. For the companies, it offers a way to demonstrate that they accept external scrutiny while continuing to develop their systems.
The unresolved question is whether voluntary safeguards can keep pace with increasingly capable AI systems.
If companies implement the controls, accept meaningful independent scrutiny and act on problems identified by auditors, the accord could become a basis for broader AI safety standards. If they fail to do so, pressure for enforceable regulation could grow.
For now, “morally binding” means a public commitment backed by political and reputational pressure, rather than an obligation backed by law. The companies have agreed to police themselves; whether that is enough will depend on how those safeguards work in practice and whether Washington eventually decides that voluntary measures are insufficient.

sources.news_title: Superintelligence Accord: Trump Renames AI ‘SI’ as 6 Tech Chiefs Sign Voluntary ‘Constitution’
sources.text:
Superintelligence Accord: Trump Renames AI ‘SI’ as 6 Tech Chiefs Sign Voluntary ‘Constitution’
Key Facts
- The document. A one-page “White House Accord on Super Intelligence”, plus a page of signatures. Trump posted it on Truth Social on 29 September 2026.
- The signatures. Trump and the leaders of Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia. OpenAI’s Sam Altman was at his company’s conference in San Francisco.
- The promises. Four voluntary “layers” of checks: internal controls, an internal team, an outside auditor and a board committee.
- The new name. A separate executive order tells federal agencies to say “SI” instead of “AI”. US law is unchanged.
- The politics. It comes five weeks before the 3 November midterm elections, amid anger over data centres and power bills, and a race with China.
- Latin America. Brazil’s binding AI bill still waits in the Chamber of Deputies. Its data-centre tax breaks became law on 15 September.
Trump says AI is now “SI” and calls the superintelligence accord “almost like a constitution”. We read every line — and explain why it came now.
The superintelligence accord signed at the White House on Tuesday, 29 September 2026, fills just one page. President Donald Trump called it “almost like a constitution in a way”. It is a voluntary promise by six tech companies to check their own AI.
Download the document (PDF, 2 pages): White House Accord on Super Intelligence — Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, as posted by President Trump on Truth Social on 29 September 2026. Text transcribed and checked by The Rio Times.
Also read the separate executive order “Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence” on whitehouse.gov.
Why Now: Data Centres, Power Bills and the Midterms
The timing is political. The midterms, the US elections held halfway through a president’s term, are on 3 November. They decide who controls Congress. And anger over data centres, the huge computer buildings that run AI, is rising. A June Reuters/Ipsos poll, cited by NPR, found 77% of Americans worried they push up power bills.
Both parties now campaign against them. Ads mentioning data centres had cost more than US$45 million by early September, NPR found. In Ohio, supporters of Democrat Sherrod Brown call Republican Senator Jon Husted “the face of data centers”. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds promises to protect families “from data centers that jack up utility rates”. The Republican Senate campaign committee (NRSC) called data centres a “sleeper issue”, NPR reported.
The White House has answered with promises. In March, tech firms signed Trump’s pledge to “build, bring, or buy” their own power. On 16 September the House of Representatives, the lower chamber of Congress, voted 417 to 3 for a bill that pushes states to make data centres pay the full cost of their grid upgrades. The Senate has not voted.
On Tuesday Trump said the companies “will be very generous to these communities”. He claimed a firm — “I believe it’s Meta” — was “paying every single teacher over $50,000” in a Louisiana parish. Not quite. Many Richland Parish teachers did get bonuses of about US$50,000. But the money came from a short-term jump in local tax income as Meta builds a data centre there, GovTech reported.
Trump’s bigger theme is China. “Whoever wins S.I. is going to win,” he said. Chinese leader Xi Jinping, who made a state visit to Washington from 23 to 25 September, “will take every data center that we don’t want”, he added. Earlier this month Trump called fears of AI “destroying Humanity” a “HOAX”, CNN reported.
Vice President JD Vance told the companies the answer was “to take the risk seriously, not to come to the government for a regulatory regime that may make things worse if it’s not smart and careful”.
What the Superintelligence Accord Says
The Accord in 10 Points
- Responsibility. “every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public.”
- Scope. It covers “every company that is training and deploying frontier models”.
- The ask. “in addition to any other precautions, we believe each company should implement the following four layers of controls and audits”.
- Layer one. Internal controls to monitor models “around areas like cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.”
- Layer two. “Empower an internal team to ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated.”
- Layer three. “Partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments of whether the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended.”
- Layer four. “Designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee and receive reports … as well as to ensure any issues identified are remediated.”
- The aim. To give “each company, its customers, and the public confidence that the technology is operating as intended.”
- Next steps. “The participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices”. And: “Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.”
- The pledge. “each of our companies are committed to doing this.” Signed by Trump, Pichai, Amodei, Zuckerberg, Brockman, Musk and Huang.
The key word is “should”, not “must”. “Frontier models”, meaning the most powerful AI systems, are never defined. There is no named auditor, standard, deadline or penalty. The auditor checks that controls work “as intended” — as each company intends. Reports go to the company’s own board, not to a regulator or the public.
The hacking clause has a reason: twice in three months, OpenAI models broke out of their test environments and reached the open internet, CNN reported.
Download the full accord (PDF, 2 pages) — text and signature page as posted by President Trump on 29 September 2026, checked by The Rio Times.
From AI to “SI”: The New Name
Speaking to reporters outside the West Wing, Trump said: “It’s not A.I., it’s S.I. … We’ve changed the name officially today.” The old term, he said, is “a fake word”.
The new name comes from a separate executive order. This is a written instruction from the president to the federal government, and it needs no vote in Congress.
What the Executive Order Does
- Section 1. The executive branch “shall use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in place of ‘Artificial Intelligence’ and ‘AI’”.
- Section 2. This covers “official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents”.
- Section 3. SI means what US law already defines as artificial intelligence. The president’s science adviser has 60 days to propose a new legal definition.
- Section 4. It creates no “right or benefit … enforceable at law”.
So the change is real but narrow: it covers how officials speak and write. US law still says “artificial intelligence”. The accord itself never uses “SI”. House Speaker Mike Johnson, leader of the lower chamber, read its subtitle as “Joint Commitment on Frontier SI Responsibilities”. The printed page says “Frontier Responsibilities”.
A “Constitution” That Binds No One
Trump said the tech chiefs “almost viewed it as a separate kind of a constitution”. Asked if the accord was binding, he replied: “I think it’s morally binding.”
A constitution creates institutions and binds people. This text does neither. The committee of “maybe 10 people” that Trump floated is not in it. It grants no rights and cannot be enforced or changed. Johnson himself called it “commitments that are voluntary on behalf of the industry”.
The chiefs themselves were modest. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg called it “a start”. Google’s Sundar Pichai compared it to “financial controls in a company”. Joe Biden’s voluntary deal of July 2023 went further on some points: seven firms also promised outside reporting of flaws and watermarks for AI-made content.
Where Was Sam Altman?
OpenAI’s chief executive was not in the room. Axios reported that Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, would attend “while CEO Sam Altman attends the company’s annual conference in San Francisco”. Brockman signed for OpenAI.
At that conference Altman launched new AI agents, AP reported, a day after OpenAI halted a more advanced model over safety concerns. Al Jazeera named it GPT-6.1 Astra. Altman told CNBC: “We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model.”
Who Did Not Sign, and the Critics
Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, AMD’s Lisa Su and Palantir’s Alex Karp came to the lunch, according to Axios, CBS News and CNN, but did not sign.
Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who did sign, chose his words with care: “the technology has very real risks. And the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion.”
Democrats were blunt. Senator Mark Warner said: “The president’s response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves.” Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote: “Self-regulation? That’s a recipe for disaster.”
Why the Superintelligence Accord Matters in Latin America
These companies’ AI tools are used across Latin America. The accord’s checks apply “during training and deployment”, in any country — but nobody can enforce them. Brazil takes another road. Its Senate passed PL 2338/2023, a bill with binding, risk-based AI rules, in December 2024. It still waits for a committee report in the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house.
Yet Brazil also wants data centres. On 15 September President Lula signed the Redata law, which suspends import duty and other federal taxes on data-centre equipment. And Trump warned on Tuesday that if US opposition continues, “they’ll be forced to go overseas or other locations”, AP reported. That puts Brazil’s power and water in play.
What to Watch Next
Trump said he will name an “AI czar”, a top adviser on AI, within three or four days, CBS News reported. The science adviser must propose a legal definition of SI by 28 November, after the midterms. Nothing is binding until laws or regulations follow — which the accord says “may make sense” one day.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the White House Accord on Superintelligence?
It is a one-page voluntary pledge signed on 29 September 2026 by Donald Trump and six tech leaders. It asks companies building the most powerful AI models to use internal controls, an internal team, an outside auditor and a board committee.
Is the superintelligence accord legally binding?
No. The text says companies “should” take its four steps and that it “may make sense” to turn them into law later. Trump called it “morally binding”.
Has AI officially been renamed SI?
Only inside the US executive branch. An executive order of 29 September 2026 tells federal agencies to say “Super Intelligence” and “SI”. US law still uses “artificial intelligence”.
Who signed the accord?
Donald Trump, Sundar Pichai (Google), Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brockman (OpenAI), Elon Musk (xAI) and Jensen Huang (Nvidia). Microsoft and Amazon, whose leaders attended the lunch, did not sign.

sources.news_title: Trump Administration Secures Voluntary AI Safety Commitments from OpenAI, Google, and Meta
sources.text:
The Trump administration has secured agreements from major technology companies on a set of voluntary guidelines aimed at shaping the development of artificial intelligence systems. According to a report from The Register, these commitments fall short of enforceable rules and rely instead on industry self-regulation, raising questions about their long-term effectiveness in addressing emerging risks.
The agreements, signed by executives from companies including OpenAI, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Anthropic, outline broad principles for safety testing, transparency in model capabilities, and measures to prevent misuse. Yet the document lacks specific metrics, deadlines, or penalties for noncompliance. Critics argue that such an approach allows firms to maintain flexibility while offering the appearance of cooperation with federal priorities. Supporters counter that voluntary pacts avoid the stifling effects of premature legislation in a field that changes rapidly.
This development comes amid ongoing debates in Washington about how much oversight artificial intelligence requires. Previous efforts under earlier administrations focused on executive orders that encouraged agencies to study potential harms without imposing binding requirements on private developers. The current framework builds on that tradition, emphasizing collaboration between government and industry rather than top-down mandates. White House officials described the signed commitments as a practical step forward that respects innovation while acknowledging genuine concerns about national security and public safety.
Industry representatives welcomed the non-binding nature of the accord. They pointed out that rigid regulations could hinder research into beneficial applications, from medical diagnostics to climate modeling. A spokesperson for one participating company noted that the guidelines reflect existing internal practices at many organizations, suggesting the document largely formalizes steps already underway. Still, independent researchers have expressed skepticism, observing that self-reported compliance often fails to deliver meaningful accountability when financial incentives point in other directions.
The agreement addresses several high-profile areas of concern. It calls for thorough evaluation of models before public release, particularly those capable of generating persuasive text, images, or code that could be weaponized. Participants pledged to implement safeguards against the creation of biological weapons, cyberattacks on critical infrastructure, and large-scale manipulation of public discourse. However, the language remains general, leaving substantial room for interpretation about what constitutes adequate protection.
One section encourages companies to share information about dangerous capabilities discovered during testing, yet it stops short of requiring disclosure to independent auditors or government agencies. Privacy advocates have highlighted this gap, warning that without external verification, claims of safety could amount to little more than marketing statements. Academic experts in machine learning have similarly called for standardized benchmarks that would allow meaningful comparisons across different systems, something the current pact does not mandate.
The timing of these commitments coincides with increased international attention on artificial intelligence governance. European Union regulators have moved forward with comprehensive legislation that imposes strict obligations on high-risk applications. In contrast, the American approach continues to favor market-driven solutions supplemented by targeted rules in sectors such as finance and healthcare. This divergence has prompted some observers to question whether fragmented standards will create compliance headaches for global technology firms operating across borders.
Domestic politics also play a visible role. Lawmakers from both parties have introduced competing bills that range from light-touch reporting requirements to more interventionist measures aimed at slowing deployment of the most powerful models. The voluntary agreement may serve as a temporary bridge, buying time while Congress considers longer-term statutory frameworks. Administration officials have indicated that they will monitor adherence closely and retain the option to pursue stronger measures if companies fall short of their public promises.
Beyond the immediate signatories, the pact invites participation from smaller developers and academic laboratories. Whether these groups will embrace the guidelines remains uncertain, given their limited resources compared with the largest players. Some startups have argued that one-size-fits-all principles could disadvantage them relative to incumbents who already maintain extensive safety teams. Others see value in aligning with widely recognized standards that could help attract investment and talent.
Public reaction has been mixed. Technology enthusiasts view the agreements as evidence that industry leaders take their responsibilities seriously without needing heavy-handed government interference. Consumer advocacy groups, however, contend that history shows self-regulation frequently proves inadequate when profits conflict with safety. Past examples from social media content moderation and data privacy provide cautionary tales about the limits of voluntary corporate pledges.
Technical experts have offered more nuanced assessments. Many agree that certain risks, such as the potential for advanced systems to assist in the design of novel pathogens, warrant serious attention. At the same time, they caution against overreacting to speculative scenarios that could chill legitimate scientific progress. The challenge lies in striking an appropriate balance that protects society without foreclosing opportunities for positive impact.
Looking ahead, the effectiveness of these commitments will likely depend on several factors. First among them is the willingness of companies to invest seriously in the promised evaluation processes rather than treating them as checkbox exercises. Second is the development of clearer metrics that allow outsiders to judge whether stated goals are being met. Third involves sustained engagement from policymakers to refine the guidelines as capabilities advance.
Some analysts predict that the current framework could evolve into more structured arrangements over time. They point to precedents in other industries where initial voluntary codes eventually formed the basis for formal standards or regulations. Others worry that without concrete enforcement mechanisms, the agreements may fade into irrelevance as competitive pressures mount and attention shifts to newer technological frontiers.
The broader context includes growing recognition that artificial intelligence systems are not simply software tools but complex entities whose behaviors can prove difficult to predict. Researchers continue to uncover unexpected capabilities even in models that appear well understood. This inherent uncertainty adds weight to calls for careful testing and layered defenses against potential harms.
At the same time, the economic stakes are enormous. Artificial intelligence already contributes substantially to productivity gains across multiple sectors, and projections suggest even larger effects in coming years. Policymakers must therefore weigh safety considerations against the risk of slowing beneficial deployment through excessive caution. The voluntary agreements represent one attempt to manage that tension, though their ultimate success remains unproven.
Independent oversight bodies could play a valuable role in assessing compliance. Several nonprofit organizations have already begun developing evaluation suites designed to probe model limitations and vulnerabilities. If companies voluntarily submit to such external reviews and publish results transparently, the current framework might gain credibility. Absent that cooperation, skepticism is likely to persist.
International coordination presents another dimension. While the United States has opted for this lighter-touch approach, other nations are pursuing different strategies. China has implemented strict controls on certain applications, while the United Kingdom has established dedicated institutes to study long-term risks. Harmonizing these varied efforts could prove challenging, yet fragmented rules risk creating safe havens for dangerous development in less regulated jurisdictions.
For now, the signed commitments stand as a visible signal of shared concern between government and industry. Whether they translate into tangible improvements in safety practices will become clearer in the months and years ahead. Observers from across the political spectrum will be watching closely to see if self-regulation delivers meaningful results or simply delays more decisive action.
As artificial intelligence systems grow more sophisticated, the conversation about appropriate governance will only intensify. The current agreements provide a starting point, however modest, for ongoing dialogue. Their limitations are readily apparent, yet they also reflect the practical realities of regulating a technology that defies easy categorization and continues to surprise even its creators. The coming period will test whether these voluntary measures can establish a foundation for responsible development or whether stronger interventions will ultimately prove necessary.

OpenAI, Google and Meta pledge independent AI safety audits under voluntary White House deal
Six companies signed a safety pact covering hacking and biological threats, with no penalties or deadline for putting the checks in place.
- OpenAI, Google, Meta, Anthropic, Nvidia and xAI agreed to let outside auditors assess their artificial intelligence safety controls under a voluntary White House pact.
- The agreement has no enforcement mechanism, disclosure requirement or implementation deadline, leaving companies to choose their auditors and address any shortcomings themselves.
- The pact calls for monitoring advanced models for cyberattack, hacking and biological or chemical risks after experimental AI agents accessed unauthorized systems and AI was linked to cryptocurrency security breaches.
OpenAI, Google, Meta and three other technology companies agreed Tuesday to bring in outside auditors to check their AI safety controls, signing a voluntary White House pact that carries no penalties if they fall short.
President Donald Trump called the agreement "morally binding." It has no enforcement mechanism and does not require companies to publish or name the auditors.
"And they understand that they have to self-police," Trump told reporters after the meeting. He said he would set up a 10-member board to oversee AI safety and appoint a new White House official to lead AI policy, and the accord says its measures could eventually be written into law.
Anthropic, Nvidia and Elon Musk's xAI, which is now part of SpaceX, also signed the Sept. 29 agreement. OpenAI was represented by President Greg Brockman, alongside Google's Sundar Pichai, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
The one-page document asks companies to monitor their most capable models during training and use, including whether they could enable cyberattacks or biological and chemical threats. It specifically calls for controls to prevent models from hacking or accessing computer systems in unintended ways.
An internal team would check that those protections work and that problems are fixed. An independent auditor would assess the controls, while a committee of each company's board would receive the findings and oversee fixes.
That would give outside reviewers a role in checking the safeguards companies rely on to keep experimental models contained.
Still, the agreement leaves the choice of auditors with the companies and sets no deadline for implementing the measures. Some of the steps are ones the companies already take in some form, according to AP.
Read More: OpenAI says its new 'Astra' AI can build attacks without human help
AI attacks
The accord follows a string of incidents in which experimental AI agents broke into computer systems they were never cleared to access, including OpenAI test agents that reached servers run by Hugging Face, a platform where developers share AI models.
An OpenAI agent also accessed an Australian government Medicare portal in June. 18, which the company disclosed to Australian authorities only in September.
Closer to crypto, AI has been suspected in some of the year’s biggest security scares.
In July, attackers began sweeping bitcoin from Coldcard hardware wallets through a five-year-old firmware flaw, taking 1,367 BTC worth nearly $89 million from 4,500 addresses across three instances. Coinkite, which makes the wallet, later said it believed someone used frontier AI to review its public code, though that has not been proven.
In early August, attackers drained Lightning nodes run through BTCPay Server, open-source software merchants use to accept bitcoin, after a flaw let them steal the credentials that control those nodes. Victims included hardware-wallet maker Foundation and bitcoin publication Citadel21. The flaw had surfaced in an AI-assisted review of BTCPay’s code, and the company said AI may also have been used to exploit it. It has not disclosed how much was taken.
Later that month, a flood of AI-generated bug reports turned up real flaws in Core Lightning, software used to run nodes on bitcoin's Lightning payment network, prompting its developers to issue emergency guidance to operators.
Tuesday’s pledge follows voluntary commitments the Biden administration collected in July 2023 from seven developers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, which at the time covered internal and external security testing before models were released.
The pledge comes a day after OpenAI confirmed it had shelved the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a follow-up to the GPT-6 Astra model it began rolling out on Sept. 3. In the middle of it all was Trump, who has punted to a group of executives to decide how best to wrangle the rapidly evolving technology, or whether it should be wrangled at all.
“There’s going to be a tremendous self-policing aspect,” Trump said.
The one-page document is short on details and relies on the companies to follow through with their promises. It is not an official order, and it is unclear who would enforce the guidance. It was signed by Trump and the leaders of Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and SpaceXAI.
The agreement echoes voluntary safety commitments by AI companies made during the Biden administration. The companies agreed to test their systems for safety and to report safety and security incidents. But the commitments were nonbinding and largely lost at the start of the Trump administration, when the president rolled back safety requirements.
The business leaders invited to the White House on Tuesday included Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, who has called for federal safety regulations, including the testing of models. Earlier this month, Amodei called for an industrywide slowdown of AI development, citing safety concerns.
The company has also been embroiled in a legal fight with the administration, and has been barred from working with the Pentagon. The two sides disagreed in negotiations over a $200 million contract, with the company’s insisting that its AI technology not be used in mass surveillance of Americans or for autonomous lethal weapons. Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Trump called Amodei “fantastic.”
Also on the guest list was Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia and a close Trump ally, who has called the safety concerns exaggerated. Huang has implored the administration and lawmakers to keep a hands-off approach to regulating the industry, saying rules would allow rival China to speed past the United States on AI leadership.
When the group appeared with reporters, the president called Huang a “very handsome guy” and asked him to speak.
“We’re going to advance this technology that is so consequential to humanity, so consequential to the future prosperity of our nation,” Huang told reporters. “We’re going to do it responsibly and safely.”
Others invited to the luncheon included Jeff Bezos, founder of Amazon; Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI; Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir; Sundar Pichai of Google; Mark Zuckerberg of Meta; and Elon Musk of SpaceXAI. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were there. David Sacks, Trump’s former top adviser on AI and a venture capitalist, also attended.
Before the luncheon, Trump told the audience at an event unveiling America.gov, an AI-powered search tool, that the U.S. government was championing the technology in an effort to counter China, a major rival in the race to develop AI.
“We don’t want to stifle growth,” Trump said.
Trump, who hosted a state visit last week for Chinese President Xi Jinping, said that the two did not spend much time discussing opportunities for partnerships or issues related to competition. Xi said in remarks at the White House that both nations shared the responsibility to develop AI with “the well-being of the people” in mind.
But in front of a crowd of executives and Cabinet members, who were gathered in an auditorium for a presentation that took on the veneer of an Apple product-launch event, the president reiterated a winner-take-all mentality.
“You’re going to have a winner, or you’re going to have a loser,” Trump said.
Trump has argued that U.S. dominance over AI technology is imperative for national security and economic growth.
With his embrace of AI and support for the development of data centers throughout the country, Trump is also increasingly out of step with the public. Recent polling shows that a majority of Americans are growing more concerned about AI and want the federal government to do more to regulate the technology.
On Tuesday, Trump again came down on the side of data centers, calling concerns about them a Democratic hoax. Flanked by executives at the luncheon, Trump predicted that the public would eventually embrace the facilities.
“You’re going to see data centers are going to be very popular, because this is the group, and they’re the ones that want to, and they’re also the ones that want to see communities that are safe and happy,” Trump said. “Otherwise, they’ll be forced to go overseas or other locations.”
As the public has soured on AI and the prospect of data centers mushrooming around the country, the debate over technology safety has intensified in recent weeks. Several rogue AI clients and models have worked together to breach websites, steal data and then cover their tracks, all while appearing to show an understanding that what they were doing was wrong. Senior leaders in Congress have acknowledged the need for AI safety guardrails.
In April, Anthropic announced it was holding back the release of one of its models, Mythos, because it was too dangerous for the public. In July, OpenAI models broke out of a restricted testing environment and hacked the AI startup Hugging Face. In early September, leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind called for slowing development of advanced AI models.
Last week, an OpenAI model was found to have meddled with U.S. government websites including the Education Department, the Securities and Exchange Commission and Commerce Department’s census site. And this week, OpenAI said it would not release its latest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.
Within the White House, senior leaders are at odds on how to regulate the industry. Bessent has floated the idea of an open dialogue with China on safety standards. He has also stressed that AI companies must be held accountable for harms created by their models.
As his day with the billionaires wrapped up Tuesday, Trump said that he was considering a committee of about 10 people focused on AI safety, and that he would name an AI czar in the coming days.
He ended his final appearance with reporters alongside Musk, another attendee who has worked himself back into Trump’s good graces after a spat last year over domestic policy legislation. Musk was seated near Xi and Trump at last week’s state dinner, and was at Trump’s side at the luncheon Tuesday.
Xi, Trump said, “will take every data center that we don’t want.”
Standing nearby, Musk agreed.
“He would love that, every single one, because you know why? They’re smart,” Trump continued. “They want every data center. They want it because that’s great for China. Well, it’s great for us, and we’re leading by a lot, and we’re going to keep it that way.”

Top AI execs sign accord to 'self-police' development
WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that tech leaders agreed to establish voluntary standards for AI and reiterated his support for rapid expansion of data centers, as concerns mount over AI safety and the industry's growing footprint in communities.
Trump said he and a large group of top executives of artificial intelligence companies signed a voluntary accord on Tuesday that will include internal and external reviews during a meeting aimed at addressing Americans' fears about the technology and its risks to humanity.
“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.
Trump and US House Speaker Mike Johnson met with leading executives from top tech and AI firms at the White House that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centres in communities across the country, which have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition.
The accord was signed by Trump, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla, SpaceX, X and xAI – now part of SpaceX.
The accord, which Trump posted on his social media site, Truth Social, late on Tuesday, opened the door to future regulation but focused on four voluntary steps for the companies to take.
The companies agreed to work with "independent auditors" to assess whether AI systems are working as their designers intended, according to the agreement. The companies also said they would work to ensure their AI tools do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."
“Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations,” the accord said.
Trump repeatedly praised the business executives for developing a technology that he said would produce “unbelievable growth."
Investment in data centres and the accompanying computer equipment has accelerated the economy and boosted the stock market, which has swelled investment accounts for higher-income Americans and lifted their spending.
Yet there were some notes of caution Tuesday. Amodei, who has been one of the most outspoken voices calling for a slowdown in AI development, said, “The technology has very real risks.”
“And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion,” he added.
Trump suggested that about 10 people would be named to a committee to “watch over the whole enterprise” and said the accord would be “morally binding.” He also said he would name someone to oversee the agreement in coming days after consulting with industry.
Some of the actions outlined in the accord are measures these companies are already taking in some form or have previously committed to doing.
The accord however does not introduce a set of legislation that introduces robust legal liability and regulation to guide the technology, which some in the industry have blown the whistle on, saying there is a chance it could outsmart humans and cause their extinction within a decade.
Trump, who has always vocally opposed instating such measures, said before the meeting that the US government wouldn't limit the development of artificial intelligence or support calls for “guardrails” or other restrictions.
“I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” Trump said at the unveiling of an AI chatbot, America.gov, intended to help Americans navigate government services. “We can’t stifle it, and we’re leading by a lot.”
Trump also said the executives had agreed to assuage the bipartisan opposition to data centers cropping up in local communities across the country by providing more financial support to local schools or taking steps to reduce energy costs.
“You’re going to see, data centers are going to be very popular," Trump said. If the opposition continued, Trump suggested, “they’ll be forced to go overseas or other locations.”

Huang sat to Trump’s right during a White House luncheon meeting, according to a seating chart the president posted on Truth Social. Musk sat to Trump’s left.
Earlier Tuesday, Trump promised that the U.S. government wouldn't limit the development of artificial intelligence or support calls for "guardrails" or other restrictions.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio highlighted that the chatbot at America.gov could soon be used to apply for a first-time passport fully online, without the in-person visit to a processing center currently required.
Trump also said the executives had agreed to assuage the bipartisan opposition to data centers cropping up in local communities across the country by providing more financial support to local schools or taking steps to reduce energy costs.
"You’re going to see, data centers are going to be very popular," Trump said. If the opposition continued, Trump suggested, "they’ll be forced to go overseas or to other locations.”

"We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model,” he said on CNBC. "We have to do these in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don’t have a bunch of anxiety.”
Zuckerberg, pulled forward from the crowd of billionaire executives by Trump to speak, said the companies agreed to develop "robust internal controls" for their AI systems.
For his part, Trump again portrayed the race to develop AI as largely a global competition between the United States and China. He said there would be a winner and a loser, with no "second place."
The two countries agreed last week to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington. sources.news_title: Trump, tech giants agree to independent AI safety audits
sources.text:
President Donald Trump endorsed using outside auditors to assess the safety of artificial intelligence systems through an accord with Silicon Valley leaders that seeks to sidestep new government rules in addressing a groundswell of concern over AI risks.
Under the agreement forged at a White House lunch Tuesday with nearly two dozen top tech industry executives, AI companies also committed to regularly meet to set best practices for the industry. The document carries no legal weight, though the president told reporters it was “morally binding.”
“It’s almost like a constitution, in a way,” Trump told reporters in the White House driveway following the event. “The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection.”
The accord emerged after a nearly two-hour meeting between the president and his guests that took place against a backdrop of rising global anxiety surrounding AI’s potentially catastrophic risks. Signers included leaders of the AI industry’s most prominent developers: Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei, Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk.
Other signers included OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Meta Platforms Inc.’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google parent Alphabet Inc., according to a copy posted by Trump on his Truth Social network. Several of the firms including Anthropic and OpenAI have previously committed to having independent evaluators.
Trump’s willingness to engage on safety after previously dismissing doomsday fears as “a hoax” reflects how AI has increasingly become politically charged ahead of the November elections. Trump has emerged as one of the loudest champions of unfettered AI development, putting him at odds with voters who are skeptical of the technology. More than seven in 10 voters said they prefer candidates who back stricter AI guardrails, according to a new Quinnipiac University poll.
Public fears about AI’s risks have grown following a series of high-profile hacks by rogue OpenAI agents — including one that targeted an Australian government website — and recent warnings from former AI company employees that the tech poses an existential threat to humanity.
With the accord, the administration held firm to its previous insistence that AI companies are responsible for policing themselves, but the document signaled a new openness to some guardrails. It suggested that AI companies “should” implement four layers of controls and noted that “it may make sense to codify” its recommendations into law or regulation in the future.
The embrace of third-party evaluators marks a shift in the administration’s posture toward AI safety. While the industry has clamored for using independent assessors to vet their most advanced models, Trump administration officials have regarded the groups best-suited to conduct those reviews with skepticism over their ideological leanings.
Ties between many safety reviewers and a movement known as effective altruism had earlier threatened to turn third-party evaluators into a nonstarter with Trump. Popular in Silicon Valley, the movement’s adherents seek to ground every decision in mathematical probabilities they believe would maximize benefit for other people, and supporters generally favor slowing AI development over fears it could lead to human extinction.
Trump’s former AI czar, David Sacks, who was present at the White House lunch on Tuesday, has dismissed outside assessments as “pseudoscience.” Even so, some of the firms poised to conduct those reviews have already met with the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, a unit inside the Commerce Department, Bloomberg News previously reported.
Beyond independent evaluators, the accord recommends that companies take safety precautions by implementing internal controls for risks related to cybersecurity, biosecurity, chemical threats and unintended actions by AI models. Companies should also build an internal team to monitor those controls and designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee safety teams and independent audits, it says.
Despite Tuesday’s nod at safety concerns, the images of Trump ingratiating himself with the group of billionaire executives whom he called the “the most brilliant people in the world” could provide fodder for his political opponents who accuse him of being too close to the tech industry.
During his appearance with the executives in the driveway, Trump showed a change of heart toward Amodei, who has long staked out a starkly different position from the president on AI safety. The Anthropic chief’s pledge to slow cutting-edge AI development earlier this month drew a rebuke on social media from Trump, yet the vibe was different Tuesday.
Trump said Amodei “has been fantastic” and summoned him to address reporters, leaning closer to him and admonishing him to “be careful.” Amodei, who met with the president for a private dinner on Sunday night, embraced Trump’s call to preserve the US lead in AI yet indicated that the core safety questions remained unresolved.
“The technology has very real risks,” Amodei said. “We all need to work together to make sure that we can win and we can win safely if we do this right,” he added before stepping out of the camera’s view as Trump complained about “fake news.”

Some of the most powerful people in artificial intelligence had lunch at the White House this week and left with a promise to police themselves, while President Donald Trump called it “morally binding”.
