sources.text:
Takeaways from Trump's summit with AI leaders
NPR's Michel Martin speaks with AI policy expert Aalok Mehta about President Trump's AI Summit with tech industry leaders.
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:
For more on President Trump's AI summit, we've called Aalok Mehta. He directs AI projects and research at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. He previously served as the responsible AI policy lead at Google. Good morning. Thanks for joining us.
AALOK MEHTA: Thanks for having me.
MARTIN: As we just heard from Emily, President Trump said that AI leaders agreed that there should be, quote, "tremendous self-regulation" at AI companies. And he said that there's already regulation by the FBI and DOJ. Can you tell us what that might look like?
MEHTA: Yeah. So in this new accord that the AI companies signed, they agreed to four levels of oversight. So essentially, they'll implement robust internal controls. And then they will have progressively layered sets of oversight, including new measures like having an independent evaluator inside the companies and having more oversight directly from company boards. And what this is doing is building on top of a number of sort of measures that companies have already taken voluntarily to address risk from their models.
MARTIN: But - OK. But what's the enforcement mechanism, other than President Trump saying it would be, quote, "morally binding" for companies to monitor their AI models?
MEHTA: There are laws on the books. So the primary law that would apply here is that the FTC has authority to regulate unfair and deceptive trade practices. And so what happens is when a company publicly commits to doing something, they have then sort of signaled to the world that that is their intent. And the FTC can then say that if the company doesn't follow through on its promises, it is acting in a deceptive way. And so this is the primary enforcement mechanism that I'm aware of that can be used when a company says it does something and then doesn't follow through on those commitments.
MARTIN: I understand. But what is the company's incentive to do that, other than - oops?
MEHTA: They have lots of incentives. I think the biggest incentive is that they want people to use their technology. They want people in the U.S. to use their technology, and they want people around the world to use their technology. And people will feel more comfortable doing that if they trust that the product they're using is safe and that they trust the company that is issuing that product. And if you look at polling around the U.S. and in other places in the world, like Europe, right now people are very skeptical about AI. They're skeptical about - that it will make their lives better. And so part of this is driven by the fact that they want to build trust in the underlying technology.
I think part of it is also because a lot of people at these companies genuinely worry about these things. In many cases, they have access to models that are more advanced than the public. And so they're seeing things that we haven't seen yet. And so that is also part of the - part of what is driving these decisions and part of what is underlying their thinking.
MARTIN: So - well, a couple questions about that, though. More broadly, is the government equipped to independently evaluate AI model safety and effectiveness?
MEHTA: In this case, they are largely relying on the companies to sort of implement these measures themselves as a form of self-regulation. And as we heard from the Anthropic CEO, there are lots of details to be figured out. So part of the work that will happen over the next months and years is for companies to figure out how to implement this in a way that is robust and useful and actually addresses safety issues. I think the thought is maybe in the future, this could become enshrined in some sort of regulation or law, but that is not contemplated right now in the near future.
There are various parts of the government that can help provide technical insights. So there's, for example, an institute within the Department of Commerce that has technical talent and does do testing on AI models. And it's unclear how that testing will factor into what the companies are going to be implementing.
MARTIN: Well, before we let you go, I think you note - and polling has indicated - that there's a lack of public trust in this technology and in these companies at this moment. But there were no AI safety groups or independent regulators present at the White House meeting. You know, there's a saying in Washington - personnel is policy. But what does that tell us?
MEHTA: It tells us - it's really consistent with the way that the Trump administration has approached the AI industry basically since the administration started, which is that its primary concern is competition with China. And it really wants to remove obstacles to the development of AI because it - the administration is concerned that any regulations will slow down the development of U.S. technology and put the U.S. at a disadvantage.
MARTIN: All right. That's Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Thank you so much.
MEHTA: Thank you.

Interestingly, it comes two weeks before the Roadster event, which was delayed due to unfavorable weather on Thursday, which could cause issues, as Tesla revealed the event must be held outdoors.
🚨 The design uses electrically driven ducted fans, typically shown as a row of four at the rear, powered by the vehicle’s high-voltage battery.

The purpose is to solve a problem that is relatively unique to high-performance electric cars. Instant motor torque is useless if the tires cannot plant that force, and conventional wings and underbody tunnels generate downforce only when air is already rushing past the car. At launch, in slow corners, and under hard braking from modest speed, passive aerodynamic additions contribute essentially very little to downforce.
Tesla’s filing says that its fans can produce the downforce needed, independent of vehicle velocity, then ease off so the same hardware does not pile on drag at highway speeds, an issue that can come from excessive body modifications.
The hardware outlined in the patent is a ducted-fan package that is placed into the rear of the vehicle. An underbody inlet between the rear wheels feeds a duct that rises to a wide outlet in the diffuser. In that outlet are four axial fans, which are divided by vertical strakes. They will pull air from under the floor and press the chassis onto the pavement.
The language in the patent claims it can cut drag rather than add to it while simultaneously increasing downforce.

The fans run from the high-voltage battery and a vehicle control system, so output can be modulated rather than left on as a fixed penalty.
There are additional strengths that can come from this design, like extra tire load at low speed, which can contribute to even more face-melting acceleration rates, decrease stopping distance, and sharper turn-in before a wing has air to work with. Adjustable fan speed lets the car add grip only when needed, so it can be catered to the force of a turn or acceleration.
These designs were previously used, and banned, in some competitive settings. The Brabham BT46B was banned in F1 competition for using a similar fan design and being labeled as too effective.
Tesla still lists the Roadster as having a sub-two-second 0-60 MPH time and a 250-plus-MPH top speed, and there are expectations for a SpaceX cold-gas thruster package that could not only increase acceleration but potentially cause the vehicle to hover.
It is important to note that a patent is not a production part, and packaging four fans in a rear diffuser, managing noise, and potential debris are all things Tesla must consider. With that being said, the patent being granted shows Tesla is designing the Roadster to go fast, but it is also attempting to use unique strategies to combat any issues it might have at those speeds.
Elon Musk
SpaceX turned a heralding moment for Starship into its greatest
Starship reached orbit despite losing an engine, deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites on Flight 14.
SpaceX’s Starship reached orbit for the first time on Monday, and for a few nail-biting minutes it looked like it wouldn’t. During ascent on Flight 14, one of Ship 41’s six Raptor engines shut down early, and SpaceX’s livestream host Dan Huot told viewers the team had decided not to commit to orbit. Minutes later, after what Huot described as a lot of conversation in the control room, the final poll came back in favor, and a roughly 19 second burn of a single Raptor pushed the ship into orbit about 170 miles up.
The reversal matters because SpaceX had written the exit ramp into the mission plan. The company said it would only fire the orbital insertion burn if flight controllers confirmed enough backup hardware remained for the deorbit burn, a condition Teslarati laid out ahead of the flight. Losing an engine was exactly the scenario that rule was built for.
Pressing forward fits Elon Musk’s history. Falcon 1 failed three straight times before its fourth launch reached orbit in 2008, with SpaceX nearly out of money, and Starship was developed by flying prototypes until they broke. What changed this year SpaceX going public, and with $SPCX sliding below its IPO price in July when Flight 13 slipped, the short interest climbed significantly, as Teslarati reported at the time. A Starship potentially lost today with revenue generating next-gen Starlink satellites aboard would have landed directly on shareholders.
Splashdown confirmed. Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on the first orbital flight of Starship! pic.twitter.com/urjmiwnvNl
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 28, 2026
That pressure showed up after orbit. SpaceX cut a flight planned to last nearly 10 hours to about three, moving splashdown from west of Chile to the North Pacific near Hawaii. SpaceX gave no reason, though Musk said this month the company was being extremely cautious about debris risk. The single Raptor for deorbit worked, and Ship 41 completed its flip and landing burn before breaking apart in the water, an outcome SpaceX expected. Musk has structured SpaceX’s governance to shield long term bets from market pressure.
The payload is the bigger business story. Musk posted that all 26 Starlink V3 satellites deployed and are “operating nominally.” Each V3 is rated for about 1 Tbps of downlink and 160 Gbps of uplink, so this single launch adds roughly 26 Tbps, about 10 times what a Falcon 9 load of V2 Mini satellites adds. The V3 is too large for Falcon 9, making Starship the only vehicle that can build out the planned 100,000 satellite constellation, at up to 60 per flight once it reaches routine service. Unlike the 20 V3 units on Flight 13, which reentered on a suborbital path, these will raise their orbits and could begin serving customers within weeks and bring in hundreds of millions of additional dollars in projected Starlink revenue.
SpaceX has already begun winding down Falcon 9 Starlink launches from Florida in favor of Starship. Reported targets put Flight 15 as early as October 19, leaving about three weeks to diagnose Monday’s engine shutdown before the next orbital attempt.

The report also placed the announcement against growing local resistance to energy-hungry data centers and skepticism from experts who question whether competitors in a breakneck race can police themselves.
The central bargain is straightforward: keep America moving fast enough to beat China, but require the companies at the frontier to build meaningful brakes, testing and accountability into their own race.

That is the right architecture on paper, especially if it preserves America’s ability to innovate at speed. The real question is whether the reviews have genuine independence, access to the information that matters and consequences strong enough to change corporate behavior.

Trump touts AI boss pledge to self-regulate
Summary
Donald Trump said tech executives at the White House had signed a morally binding pledge to self-regulate AI in Washington on Tuesday. The accord includes internal controls, auditing, and a possible future path to laws or regulations. Trump also said he would rename the technology super intelligence, while participants such as Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk backed the industry-led approach.
Key Facts
- The lunch meeting included Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Jeff Bezos, Satya Nadella and Sundar Pichai.
- The White House Accord is described as not legally enforceable but leaves room to codify the steps into laws or regulations over time.
- Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg said the accord is meant to reassure customers that AI works as intended and called it a starting point for industry-wide standards.
- Elon Musk said the executives agreed to grade each other’s homework, which he said is better than each company grading only its own.
- Of the 31 guests, only two were women: Susie Wiles and Lisa Su of AMD.
WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the tech executives gathered at the White House to discuss regulating AI had signed a "morally binding" commitment to build adequate safeguards on the fast-moving technology.
"They're going to police themselves," Trump said after the meeting that gathered the top leaders in artificial intelligence, including Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei.
Trump said the tech bosses had signed a deal that would put on paper their commitment to self-regulate in a morally binding agreement that would not be legally enforceable.
But the final document, dubbed the White House Accord, left the door open "to codify these steps into laws or regulations" if it made sense over time.
Speaking to reporters outside the Oval Office surrounded by the world's most powerful tech bosses, Trump also confirmed that he would officially rename the technology "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence "because it's not artificial."
Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg said the accord aims to assure customers that AI technology "works in the way that we intend."
The commitment includes "robust internal controls" and multiple layers of auditing -- from internal risk reviews to external auditors and oversight from the companies' boards of directors, he said.
Zuckerberg called it a starting point for industry-wide standards.
Elon Musk said the executives essentially agreed to "grading each other's homework, which is a lot better than if people just grade their own homework for obvious reasons."
The lunch meeting also included Jeff Bezos, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sundar Pichai of Google.
Of the 31 guests, two were women: Susie Wiles, Donald Trump's chief of staff, and Lisa Su, CEO of AMD.
The gathering occurred as attitudes toward AI sour in Washington, with lawmakers increasingly under pressure from voters to curb or slow AI development over fears it could displace workers and upend society.
Those concerns gained force from a run of incidents in which OpenAI's autonomous systems slipped out of their constraints, beginning with a July breach of Hugging Face — a widely used platform for sharing AI models.
OpenAI announced on Monday it was canceling the release of its latest model, known as Astra 6.1, after internal testing by the ChatGPT-maker revealed it did not meet safety standards.
Trump, advised by Huang and his former AI czar David Sacks, has urged unfettered AI development to outpace China and fuel a U.S. economy increasingly dependent on AI-driven growth.
The issue of data centers, the vast computing facilities the technology requires, has emerged as a flashpoint in midterm election races in both parties, with more and more communities worried about rising electricity bills and the strain on water and land.
Trump has dismissed opponents of these data centers and after the meeting insisted that AI companies "will be very generous" with communities who open their doors to them.
"They'll help with their schools, they'll help with their teachers," he said.
'Still under discussion'
Major AI companies, particularly Anthropic and OpenAI, have issued stark public warnings about uncontrolled development of increasingly powerful systems — even as they develop and deploy this same state-of-the-art technology.
Those concerns intensified after a former employee of both companies went public with warnings that the industry is moving faster than safety reviews allow.
Anthropic warned investors of potential existential risks to humanity in the prospectus for its highly anticipated initial public offering, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.
Anthropic is aiming for an IPO as early as November.
Trump has repeatedly characterized these warnings about existential risks as overblown and the White House has bitterly clashed with Anthropic over AI safety.
"As the president has said whoever wins AI, wins. I think that's very important," Amodei said after the meeting. "But I think the technology has very real risks, and the mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion."

sources.news_title: Trump floats fresh data center "dividend" after meeting AI tech leaders
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said that Americans living in a community with a data center could receive a "dividend," adding that residents will benefit "greatly" from the centers, while speaking with reporters on Tuesday.
The president has touted artificial intelligence in the past and even rebranded it "super intelligence" on Tuesday, saying that AI is a "fake word." The administration has been an advocate for states and communities to welcome the centers as well as pushing for the U.S. to grow its capabilities on artificial intelligence.
"The people are going to benefit directly, whether its teachers that get paid a bonus, whether its people that live in the community that get paid a dividend you could call it a dividend because a dividend sounds right, they are going to greatly benefit by what's happened," Trump said in part.
"Data centers are bringing in a tremendous amount of money into the community, and the people now are going to benefit directly," the president added.
Trump has previously floated the idea of Americans getting dividend checks, most recently during the RNC Midterm Convention. He suggested that people would benefit if Republicans secured the majority during the midterm elections because of possible economic prosperity.
The White House referred Newsweek to Trump's remarks when reached for comment Tuesday evening.
What To Know
Trump's comments come as Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon and other lawmakers have questioned or floated ideas for distributing funds to communities impacted by data centers.
"Do we do what they do in Alaska, which is like, they give dividends to people who are impacted by the pipeline?" Nixon told Newsweek last week in a wide-ranging interview. "Do we do the same thing for the now existing AI data centers?" Similar ideas have been suggested by other lawmakers including Independent Senator Bernie Sanders, for Americans to receive payments via a federally managed “AI sovereign wealth fund."
AI and data centers have been somewhat of a flashpoint during the lead up to the midterms, as lawmakers have more and more vocalized their position on the potential dangers or advantages of the technology. Trump has been an avid supporter of data center growth arguing that communities rejecting the centers risk economic stagnancy, saying the projects can bring jobs and lower taxes.
The president also announced the launch of America.gov on Tuesday, in what the administration frames as a new AI-powered portal to federal services and information. The site is aimed at streamlining the public's interactions with the U.S. government.
Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University told Newsweek on Tuesday in part, "Trump wants data centers built here, not overseas, and local backlash is now the biggest speed bump."
"Talking about dividends for host communities is a way to sell that buildout to voters who see higher power bills and no direct benefit. The midterm $5,000 check was a national campaign pitch. This is a narrower pitch aimed at towns that can stop projects. There is a real economic idea underneath it, sharing tax revenue or company payouts with neighbors, but the timing and the word dividend tell you he is also trying to turn a land use fight into a pocketbook message," Agranoff added. 
"Being pro data centers and promising checks to the people who live next to them is how he tries to keep both the industry and the electorate on side," Agranoff concluded. 
Tech Leaders Convene at White House
Meanwhile, the president hosted numerous leaders in technology on Tuesday including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner.
The meeting occurred alongside the launch of America.gov and comes on the heels of a state dinner to honor Chinese President Xi Jinping last week where numerous tech leaders attended.
Industry leader Bill Gates also recently warned in part that AI could certainly be powerful enough " to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths."

Trump, tech bosses sign voluntary pact pledging ‘robust’ AI safeguards
US President Trump touts self-regulation amid calls from the international community and industry for formal rules.
United States President Donald Trump and top tech executives have signed an accord promising greater safeguards for artificial intelligence amid growing concerns that the frontier technology is exposing humanity to catastrophic risks.
Trump announced the voluntary accord on Tuesday after gathering AI leaders at the White House for a luncheon event that reaffirmed his administration’s scepticism of government regulation of the rapidly advancing technology.

“There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that,” Trump said while seated alongside tech executives.
Under the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, bosses at Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia pledged to implement “robust” controls to monitor AI models and appoint internal teams to “ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated”.
The companies also pledged to partner with independent external auditors to ensure the safeguards are working as intended and to meet regularly to “establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems”.
The accord, which does not stipulate who would carry out third-party evaluations, states that it “may make sense” to codify the measures into law or formal regulations in the future.
“Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this,” the accord states.
‘Pace the frontier’
The six signatories are Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, Google’s Sundar Pichai, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, xAI’s Elon Musk, and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.
The accord comes as the Trump administration is at odds with calls for urgent action to regulate AI from both the international community and key industry figures, including Anthropic’s Amodei, who has urged developers to slow down and “pace the frontier”.
Twenty countries and the European Union last week issued a call for global coordination to ensure AI remains under human control, including the potential creation of an oversight body to set and enforce standards.
Trump has rejected calls for supranational regulation, telling the United Nations General Assembly last week that his administration would oppose “any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” AI.
Trump has also dismissed calls from the industry for a slowdown in development, despite warnings of catastrophic and even existential risks, citing the need to maintain a lead over China.
The risks of AI escaping human control have received scrutiny following a slew of cases of AI agents going rogue and conducting cyberattacks on organisations and government agencies.
On Monday, OpenAI announced that it would not release its latest AI model after identifying safety risks during in-house testing.
The creator of ChatGPT also separately issued a public apology for its handling of a series of incidents in which its AI agents gained unauthorised access to Australian government websites, including a national healthcare database.
Trump’s accord drew a mixed response on Tuesday, with critics noting its nonbinding nature and limited details.
Silicon Valley investor David Sacks, who previously served as Trump’s AI tsar, called the accord “far better” than an international agreement that would “probably never happen”.
“President Trump continues to ensure that the U.S. remains the technology leader while putting Americans first,” Sacks said in a post on X.
Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, welcomed the pledge by industry leaders but said it fell far short of what was needed.
“The most serious risk to Americans is not a Chinese superintelligence. It is a smaller model in non-state hands, used for biological, chemical, or cyber-harm,” Graylin told Al Jazeera.
“Putting that on paper, with Zuckerberg and Huang in the room alongside Amodei, is better than another year of ‘we cannot regulate because China will not’,” Graylin said.
“What is missing is independence and anything that crosses a border. The companies drafted the principles, they hire the auditor, and the commitment is voluntary, on a day the White House also said it would not support guardrails,” he added.
‘Incompetent and careless’
Toby Walsh, chief at the UNSW AI Institute in Sydney, Australia, said AI companies had already proven “incompetent and careless at managing themselves”.
“What other trillion-dollar industry marks its own homework?” he told Al Jazeera.
“It’s too tempting to cut corners,” Walsh said, adding that top executives should be held liable for the harms caused by their products.
“We should be billing them for all the time put into identifying and fixing these cyberattacks,” he said.
David Krueger, an AI expert at the University of Montreal who advocates a pause in development, criticised the accord as vague and a further example of the Trump administration’s reliance on self-regulation.
“The Trump administration is continuing its ‘regulate without regulating’ approach, where everything is ostensibly voluntary, but there is an implicit threat of punishment for noncompliance,” Krueger told Al Jazeera.
“If you look at the substance, it’s interesting that it calls for external evaluators, so it might result in a minute improvement over the status quo,” Krueger said.
“But I’m not excited by something that might reduce the risk by 1 percent.”

Trump, AI CEOs sign voluntary safety pact, back data center expansion
WASHINGTON >> President Donald Trump today said tech executives agreed to establish voluntary standards for AI and reiterated his support for rapid expansion of data centers, as concerns mount over AI safety and the industry’s growing footprint in communities.
Trump made the comments after meeting with tech executives at the White House. The companies agreed to work with “independent auditors” to assess whether AI systems are working as their designers intended, according to a copy of the agreement posted by Trump on his social media platform. The companies also said they would work to ensure their AI tools do not “hack or access technical systems in unintended ways.”
The administration faces increasing scrutiny over risks posed by advanced AI, after OpenAI and Anthropic reported their AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into other companies’ systems.
Data centers, which provide the computing power to train and run AI models, have drawn opposition in communities nationwide over concerns about electricity demand, utility costs and other local impacts. The backlash poses a political challenge for Republicans heading into the US midterm elections on November 3.
“It’s almost like a constitution, in a way,” Trump said, referring to the agreement between the companies. “And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president. And it really is a form of protection.”
What began as a closed-door lunch with technology executives spilled into public view when Trump joined House Speaker Mike Johnson and a lineup of CEOs on the White House driveway, an area rarely used by the president to speak to journalists. He took questions from reporters for about 30 minutes on AI safety and other topics with the CEOs standing behind him.

The unusual scene came as pressure has mounted on the administration to address the risks and rapid spread of AI, and underscored the alliance Trump has cultivated with leaders of the tech industry. Zuckerberg, pulled forward from the crowd of billionaire executives by Trump to speak, said the companies agreed to develop “robust internal controls” for their AI systems. He added he would soon name a new official to lead White House policies on AI.

“These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities,” Trump later told reporters gathered on the White House driveway, surrounded by the company executives.
But the companies have come under fire for not doing enough to make AI safer. AI company executives and investors were among the largest individual donors in 2025 to MAGA Inc., a political action committee aligned with the president. OpenAI’s Brockman and his wife, Anna Brockman, gave a combined $25 million to the committee in 2025, according to Federal Election Commission records.
Trump met with the CEOs the same day his aides announced a new AI tool that they said will make it easier for the public to use government services.
Silicon Valley executives attended an event launching the new tool, including Meta’s Dina Powell McCormick and Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire. Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia led the design of the new tool. Silicon Valley companies Google, SpaceX, Meta and 8VC were listed in the launch event’s program as sponsors.
Trump at the launch event said the AI tool could not “in theory, be hacked into” by bad actors. He did not provide evidence.

Those concerns intensified after a former employee of both companies went public with warnings that the industry is moving faster than safety reviews allow.
Anthropic warned investors of potential existential risks to humanity in the prospectus for its highly anticipated initial public offering, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday. Anthropic is aiming for an IPO as early as November.

sources.news_title: Trump rejects new federal AI regulations, backs industry self-regulation
sources.text:
President Donald Trump shot down the idea of new federal regulations on artificial intelligence after meeting at the White House with top industry executives amid growing global concerns over threats posed by the technology.
In lieu of new rules, Trump and the executives agreed on a framework where they would partner with outside auditors to conduct safety assessments of models and implement stronger internal controls over their systems, according to a copy of an accord signed by the president and Silicon Valley leaders following a White House lunch on AI risks Tuesday.
The luncheon brought together nearly two dozen Silicon Valley leaders, including Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei and Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang. After the event, Trump said existing laws would be enough to safeguard Americans from AI’s potential risks, despite a growing nationwide backlash to the technology.
“There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that, but the self-regulation is very important,” the president told reporters in a brief appearance in the East Room with his guests.
Industry agrees to voluntary safety framework
House Speaker Mike Johnson described the document as “voluntary” set of “commitments” by the industry to implement “robust internal controls and layers of internal and external review.”
Pressure to take action has increased following high-profile security breaches by rogue AI models that fueled calls by Silicon Valley AI developers and world leaders for new standards on the technology. Yet Trump’s remarks splashed cold water on the notion that the administration might move away from its hardened opposition to new government AI safeguards and become more open to new rules.
Trump welcomed the executives for the luncheon with Johnson, joined by other technology industry attendees including Meta Platforms Inc. CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Palantir Technologies Inc. CEO Alex Karp and OpenAI President Greg Brockman. The decision to even engage on AI safety had appeared to mark a shift for Trump, who only last week rejected fears of catastrophic risk as “a hoax.”
In an impromptu appearance on the West Wing driveway after the event, Trump floated the idea of a “committee” of roughly 10 people that would help “watch over the whole enterprise.” He gave no additional details.
Silicon Valley leaders back hands-off approach
Industry leaders who joined Trump outside the White House largely endorsed the president’s desire to maintain a hands-off approach and let AI companies police themselves. Huang, whose company makes the chips that have helped power the AI boom, said that he saw “no conflict between innovation, technology, and safety.”
“We are going to have to create new technologies to advance the capabilities of AI,” said Huang, a day after Nvidia unveiled new software security tools designed to keep AI agents from going rogue. “But we’re also creating new technologies to advance the safety of AI.”
Other industry attendees included Microsoft Corp. CEO Satya Nadella, SpaceX’s Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s Lisa Su, according to a list released by the White House.
AI safety debate creates political dilemma
The AI safety debate has posed a political dilemma for Trump, who has cast himself as one of the nation’s loudest champions of AI, arguing that its unfettered development is key to beating China and sustaining the US economy. But polls show Americans have rapidly become more wary of the technology’s risks, including job loss, higher electricity costs and major cyber attacks, threatening to put Trump on the wrong side of the issue ahead of the November midterm elections.
Trump has recently become preoccupied with AI’s name, suggesting he sees the controversy surrounding the technology as a branding problem more than an issue with its potential dangers. The president later Tuesday signed an executive order requiring federal agencies to refer to the technology as “super intelligence,” an effort to counter the increasingly negative public perceptions of AI.
The president did appear to acknowledge the growing public discontent. He indicated that companies in attendance would work more closely with local communities to ease concerns over the impact of new data center construction but did not provide specifics.
Trump hosts AI leaders amid election concerns
The optics of the event, however, as Trump embraced the billionaire executives behind an unpopular industry, threatened to create new challenges for his party ahead of November’s midterm election. Populist Democrats have seized on economic discontent over high costs of living, threatening to break Republicans’ control of Congress.
When reporters entered the meeting room, the executives were lined up behind the president as if posing for a group photo and Trump gushed about their contributions to the US. Shortly before the lunch, Trump had posted a seating chart on his Truth Social network that had Huang and Musk, the world’s richest person, flanking him.
Trump and Amodei discuss AI safety
The lunch took place days after Trump met with Amodei, a move that brought together two men at opposite ends of the AI safety debate. The late-night dinner on Sunday marked their first private sit-down after months of rocky relations between the Anthropic chief and the administration over safety-related issues involving the company’s AI tools.
Amodei has long warned about AI’s existential risks, and he propelled the safety debate into the mainstream with a Sept. 12 essay, promising to slow development of the most advanced models and urging more regulation. His pledge to pace development was embraced by his rivals, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Musk, but it prompted objections from Trump who has defended pushing ahead with the technology at full speed.
During his appearance with the executives in the driveway, Trump said the Anthropic chief “has been fantastic” and summoned him to address reporters. Amodei embraced Trump’s call to preserve the US lead in AI yet indicated that the core safety questions remained unresolved.
“The technology has very real risks,” Amodei said. “We all need to work together to make sure that we can win and we can win safely if we if we do this right.”
Highlighting those concerns, OpenAI said Monday it would hold back a version of its Astra model while it establishes stronger safeguards.
Johnson has acknowledged the dire warnings coming from within the AI industry by saying that Congress “potentially” will need to impose guardrails, though he cautioned it would likely take “some time” to fashion legislation with broad enough support to pass.

sources.news_title: Trump, tech executives release 'morally binding' accord amid rising fears over AI safety
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said tech executives agreed to establish standards for AI and reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centers, as concerns mount over AI safety and the industry's growing footprint in communities.
Trump made the comments after a meeting with tech executives at the White House. The administration is facing increasing scrutiny over the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence, after OpenAI and Anthropic reported their AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into other companies' systems.
Data centers, which provide the computing power needed to train and run AI models, have drawn opposition in communities nationwide over concerns about electricity demand, utility costs and other local impacts. The backlash poses a political challenge for Republicans heading into the US midterm elections on November 3.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said, referring to the agreement between the companies. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president. And it really is a form of protection."
Trump released the one-page document on his Truth Social platform - which he had earlier described as "morally binding" - and that urged four layers of controls in companies.
First, the document asks companies to partner with an external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments of whether a company's AI control and monitoring systems were operating as intended.
Second, it urges companies to designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee and receive reports from internal and external auditors and from teams operating AI controls.
Third, it asks for internal controls to monitor capabilities and alignment of AI models during training and deployment around areas like cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats to ensure that models "do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."
And fourth, it requests that companies have an internal team to ensure "all of the controls, monitoring and detection are operating as intended."
Luncheon spills into public view
What began as a closed-door lunch with technology executives spilled into public view when Trump joined House Speaker Mike Johnson and a lineup of CEOs on the White House driveway, an area rarely used by the president. He took questions for about 30 minutes on AI safety and other topics with the CEOs standing shoulder to shoulder behind him.
The unusual scene came as pressure has mounted on the administration to address the risks and rapid spread of AI, and underscored the alliance Trump has cultivated with leaders of the tech industry. Executives at the meeting included OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Google's Sundar Pichai and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Zuckerberg, pulled forward from the crowd of billionaire executives by Trump to speak, said that the companies agreed to develop "robust internal controls" for their AI systems, adding that auditors would check those procedures and report back to company boards. Trump said he is considering setting up a 10-person board to police the safety of AI tools, without specifying who would make up that group.
The document was signed by Trump and the bosses of Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, social media platform X/Twitter, and NVIDIA.
'Makes sense' to transform steps into laws, White House says
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations. Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies is committed to doing this," the White House accord said.
"The participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems," it added.
Trump doubles down on data centers
Trump separately told reporters at the White House that the tech companies would work to make communities "happy" about the construction of data centers.
Data centers are "going to do things for the community that will be really financially beneficial," he told reporters. "These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities."
Trump met with the executives the same day his aides announced a new AI tool that they said will make it easier for the public to use government services.
Silicon Valley executives attended the launch event on Tuesday morning, including Meta's Dina Powell McCormick and Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire. Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia led the design of the new tool. Silicon Valley companies Google, SpaceX, Meta and 8VC were listed in the launch event's program as sponsors.
Trump at the launch event said he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology, adding that doing so would make it harder for US companies to build better AI products than their Chinese counterparts.
Trump also said that he discussed AI with Xi when he visited the US last week, adding that the US already works with Xi's government "in so many ways."

sources.text:
Trump says AI companies agree to 'self-police'
September 30, 2026
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said a group of CEOs of Artificial Intelligence (AI) companies had signed an accord to "self-police" the technology's development.
Trump met with AI leaders at the White House, where he doubled down on his support for the technology.
The agreement comes as public scrutiny has grown over the risks posed by the emerging technology, following reports that OpenAI and Anthropic's AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into other companies' systems.
Concerns are also mounting over the industry's growing footprint in communities, particularly with the growth of data centers.
Prior to the meeting, Trump had reiterated that his government would not limit the development of AI or support calls for "guardrails" or other restrictions on the sector.
"I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution," Trump said. "We can't stifle it, and we're leading by a lot."
Trump also announced that he would officially rename the technology "super intelligence" because "it's not artificial."
Which AI leaders were at the White House meeting?
House Speaker Mike Johnson joined the meeting, which included top AI executives like Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Elon Musk, whose X social media platform includes its own AI model, Grok.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also attended.
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police," Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.
Later, the US president posted a copy of the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence" on his Truth Social platform.
What does the AI accord say?
"Every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public," the accord begins.
The document affirms that tech companies will implement "robust internal controls to ensure all of the controls, monitoring, and detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated."
They are to "empower an internal team" to ensure "control, monitoring, and detection" are working as intended.
AI companies are also expected to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator to carry out independent assessments," as well as "designate an independent committee of the board of directors" to oversee and receive reports.
Trump said the agreement is "morally binding" but not legally enforceable.
The accord does, however, leave the door open "to codify these steps into laws or regulations."

sources.text:
President Trump just put the biggest names in artificial intelligence on the record.
They are racing to build technology powerful enough to transform the economy, national security and everyday life. Now they have signed a voluntary White House pact promising to police the risks that come with it.
After a meeting and luncheon with top technology executives Tuesday, President Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson announced what the administration calls the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.
President Trump described the agreement as “morally binding” and compared it to a constitution for the industry.
That phrase matters. The agreement creates no new federal law or sweeping regulatory regime.
It is a public commitment by the companies building the most advanced systems in the world—and a test of whether they will accept real responsibility without Washington smothering American innovation.
The White House carried the meeting live:
President Trump Participates in a Meeting and Luncheon on Super Intelligence https://t.co/RRkEnM2KDS
— The White House (@WhiteHouse) September 29, 2026
The room included leaders from Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI. Signers reportedly included Sundar Pichai, Mark Zuckerberg, Jensen Huang, Greg Brockman, Dario Amodei and Elon Musk.
The Associated Press reported that the accord calls for companies to establish internal controls, submit to outside reviews and audits, and accept independent oversight. President Trump said the companies were already showing “tremendous self-policing” and suggested that an oversight group could include roughly ten people.
The agreement was signed after a White House meeting involving Trump, Johnson and executives whose companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI infrastructure. The report also placed the announcement against growing local resistance to energy-hungry data centers and skepticism from experts who question whether competitors in a breakneck race can police themselves.
The central bargain is straightforward: keep America moving fast enough to beat China, but require the companies at the frontier to build meaningful brakes, testing and accountability into their own race.
The announcement landed late Tuesday:
Trump releases AI accord with tech executives https://t.co/oWsjQK24sy https://t.co/oWsjQK24sy
— Reuters (@Reuters) September 30, 2026
Axios described the agreement as a set of voluntary standards for reviewing powerful AI systems, including internal risk reviews and outside audits. The accord emerged after months of fierce debate over whether Washington should impose hard limits or let American companies move aggressively while China tries to catch up.
The outlet noted the obvious point of tension: people working in AI doubt that self-policing alone can control an industry whose competitors are spending staggering sums to move faster than one another. More implementation details were still expected, leaving the credibility of the accord tied to who conducts the reviews, what the companies must disclose and what happens when a signer falls short.
That concern should not be dismissed. A voluntary promise is only as strong as the people willing to enforce it when honoring the promise becomes expensive.
But the alternative cannot be a panicked Washington rulebook written by politicians and permanent bureaucrats who do not understand the technology, cannot keep pace with it and may use “safety” as an excuse to centralize control.
Speaker Johnson put the challenge in the right terms: security and innovation are not enemies.
We have a broader obligation to the people and to safety and to ensuring that this is done right and well.
Security and innovation are not mutually exclusive. You can do both. pic.twitter.com/3e6MNPE95E
— Speaker Mike Johnson (@SpeakerJohnson) September 29, 2026
Semafor reported that Johnson framed the pact around robust internal controls and layers of internal and external review. President Trump emphasized self-regulation after meeting with more than a dozen AI and technology leaders, while Johnson presented the accord as the industry’s answer to calls for stronger guardrails.
That is the right architecture on paper, especially if it preserves America’s ability to innovate at speed. The real question is whether the reviews have genuine independence, access to the information that matters and consequences strong enough to change corporate behavior.
If a model fails a serious safety test, will the public learn about it before release—or only after something goes wrong? Who chooses the outside auditors?
Can the oversight board demand changes, or can a company simply ignore it? Will every signer play by the same rules when billions of dollars and the race with Communist China are on the line?
Those details will determine whether this accord becomes a durable American standard or a handsome document that disappears the moment pressure rises.
There is also a deeper political significance here. President Trump is rejecting the false choice between surrendering the AI race and surrendering the country to an unaccountable technology cartel.
America should build, and America should lead.
America should not hand Beijing the defining technology of the century because Washington became frightened of its own innovators.
At the same time, companies asking the nation for energy, chips, data centers, government contracts and public trust owe the American people more than slogans. They owe verifiable standards, honest disclosure and consequences when those standards are broken.
The White House accord is a serious opening move. Now the signers must prove that “morally binding” means something when the easy promises end and the hard decisions begin.

Trump and Tech Leaders Sign Voluntary AI Accord
President Donald Trump and technology executives signed a voluntary AI accord at the White House on September 29, 2026. It commits companies to internal risk controls, detection capabilities, external review and board oversight. Trump called the pledge "morally binding" and "almost like a constitution." Mike Johnson said it is "voluntary on behalf of the industry." Present were Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Jeff Bezos, Satya Nadella, Lisa Su and Dario Amodei; Su told reporters she felt "very encouraged." Trump rejected stricter AI-specific regulation citing competition with China, said he will name an AI czar within three to four days, and floated renaming artificial intelligence to "super intelligence." Trump posted that communities opposing data centers want to end up "backwards and poor." A July Fox News survey found 70 percent opposed a local AI data center, including 60 percent of Republicans and 76 percent of Democrats. Candidates in at least 21 races across 18 states aired ads on data centers. JD Vance addressed the issue in Michigan, where OpenAI, Oracle and Related Digital are investing more than $7 billion in a campus. Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay urging slower AI development. OpenAI postponed GPT-6.1 Astra after safety reviews following a July 2026 cyberattack by its models on Hugging Face.

sources.text:
Trump, AI CEOs sign voluntary safety pact, back data centre expansion
- US President Donald Trump and top AI CEOs agreed on voluntary safety standards for AI, including independent audits and protections against unintended system access.
- Trump supports rapid expansion of data centres despite community concerns, promising tech companies will contribute positively to local areas.
- Trump plans to create a 10-person board to oversee AI safety and recently launched a government AI tool, instructing agencies to use the term "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence".
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump on Sept 29 said tech executives agreed to establish voluntary standards for AI and reiterated his support for rapid expansion of data centres, as concerns mount over AI safety and the industry’s growing footprint in communities.
Trump made the comments after meeting tech executives at the White House.
The companies agreed to work with “independent auditors” to assess whether AI systems are working as their designers intended, according to a copy of the agreement posted by Trump on his social media platform.
The companies also said they would work to ensure their AI tools do not “hack or access technical systems in unintended ways”.
The administration faces increasing scrutiny over risks posed by advanced AI, after OpenAI and Anthropic reported their AI agents had gone rogue and hacked into other companies’ systems.
Data centres, which provide the computing power to train and run AI models, have drawn opposition in communities nationwide over concerns about electricity demand, utility costs and other local impacts. The backlash poses a political challenge for Republicans heading into the US midterm elections on Nov 3.
“It is almost like a constitution, in a way,” Trump said, referring to the agreement between the companies. “And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as President. And it really is a form of protection.”
What began as a closed-door lunch with technology executives spilt into public view when Trump joined House Speaker Mike Johnson and a line-up of CEOs on the White House driveway, an area rarely used by the President to speak to journalists. He took questions from reporters for about 30 minutes on AI safety and other topics, with the CEOs standing behind him.
The unusual scene came as pressure has mounted on the administration to address the risks and rapid spread of AI, and underscored the alliance Trump has cultivated with leaders of the tech industry.
Executives at the meeting included OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Google’s Sundar Pichai and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.
Zuckerberg, pulled forward from the crowd of billionaire executives by Trump to speak, said the companies agreed to develop “robust internal controls” for their AI systems.
Trump said he is considering setting up a 10-person board to police the safety of AI tools. He did not specify potential members of that group. He added he would soon name a new official to lead White House policies on AI.
President doubles down on data centres
Asked whether he was concerned that his support for data centres could hurt Republicans in November, Trump said tech companies would work to make communities “happy” about the construction of data centres.
“These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities,” Trump later told reporters gathered on the White House driveway.
But the companies have come under fire for not doing enough to make AI safer. A nationwide Reuters/Ipsos poll from Sept 17 to 20 shows some 73% of respondents worry that AI companies have not done enough to prevent AI from causing serious harm to society, and 55% of people said it will be good to slow AI development.
AI company executives and investors were among the largest individual donors in 2025 to MAGA, a political action committee aligned with the President. OpenAI’s Brockman and his wife, Anna Brockman, gave a combined US$25 million (S$32 million) to the committee in 2025, according to Federal Election Commission records.
Trump met the CEOs the same day his aides announced a new AI tool that they said will make it easier for the public to use government services.
Silicon Valley executives attended an event launching the new tool, including Meta’s Dina Powell McCormick and Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire. Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia led the design of the new tool. Silicon Valley companies Google, SpaceX, Meta and 8VC were listed in the launch event’s programme as sponsors.
Trump said at the launch event that the AI tool could not “in theory, be hacked into” by bad actors. He did not provide evidence.
On Sept 29, he also directed government agencies to use the words “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence” when referring to the technology. REUTERS

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said that he and a large group of leaders from artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews during a meeting at the White House aimed at addressing Americans' fears about the technology.
“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters during an impromptu press conference outside the West Wing.
Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson met leading executives from top tech firms that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centres in communities across the country that have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition. The group included CEOs who have called for a slowdown in the development of the technology after several high-profile incidents where AI agents have gone rogue.
The accord, which Trump posted on his social media site Truth Social late Tuesday, opened the door to future regulation but focused on four voluntary steps for the companies to take.

The accord said the companies would implement “robust internal controls”, partner with an “independent external auditor” to assess whether the controls were working, and set up a committee among each company's board of directors to evaluate reports from internal and external auditors.
“Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws and regulations,” the accord said.
Trump repeatedly praised the business executives for developing a technology that he said would produce “unbelievable growth". Investment in data centres and the accompanying computer equipment has accelerated the economy and boosted the stock market, which has swelled investment accounts for higher-income Americans and lifted their spending.
Yet there were some notes of caution Tuesday. Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, who has been one of the most outspoken voices calling for a slowdown in the development of AI, said “the technology has very real risks”.

“We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model,” he said on CNBC. “We have to do these in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don’t have a bunch of anxiety.”
