sources.news_title: The Latest: Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to ‘self-police’ AI development
sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said during a meeting at the White House that he and a large group of leaders of artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews of the technology.
Trump suggested there would be about 10 people named to a committee to “watch over the whole enterprise” and said the accord would be “morally binding.”
Trump also unveiled Tuesday the AI-powered America.gov site as a way to simplify public access to government information and services. The site’s question-and-answer function initially produced truthful responses to politically thorny questions — contrary to several of Trump’s characteristic claims.
Within moments, however, the site began modifying its answers. After originally confirming that Trump’s name is in the Epstein files, that Democrat Joe Biden beat him in the 2020 election and that climate change is largely human-caused, it subsequently refused to answer the questions, saying it didn’t answer political inquiries.
Meanwhile, former Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith, who brought two federal indictments against Trump, told lawmakers Tuesday that he “will not be silenced by continued threats of prosecution” from the Trump administration and that he believes the rule of law is being threatened like never before. Smith’s hearing before the Senate is expected to focus on his team’s access to GOP lawmakers’ phone records when prosecutors were investigating Trump’s efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 election.
Here's the latest:
White House releases self-policing AI pledge that Trump says is ‘morally binding’
The president signed an executive order after holding a White House lunch meeting with top industry leaders. It mostly focuses on Trump’s insistence that artificial intelligence be called “super intelligence.”
But Trump said the document would work with industry leaders to keep AI safe for users while also not limiting innovation in the field.
The president said that officials were already “seeing tremendous self-policing” around ensuring AI doesn’t become too powerful for its own good. And he said his administration may create a 10-person committee charged with overseeing the AI industry.
Key Democratic senator criticizes Hegseth’s planned cuts of generals
Sen. Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said eliminating senior leadership positions must be done in consultation with Congress.
Pentagon officials say Hegseth plans to announce in an address Wednesday that the military needs to carry out a 20% total decrease to the roughly 800 flag and general officer positions by Jan. 1, 2027.
Reed warned that the planned cuts “should alarm every American.”
“Congress has been clear with the Secretary that he must consult this body and explain his reasoning for senior officer removals and promotion holds. To date, we have not received satisfactory answers,” Reed said in a statement.
“Our military is conducting major operations around the world, and the force is already under strain,” he added. “Eliminating senior positions and leaders now will add to that strain and disrupt command when continuity matters most.”
Hegseth set to announce more job cuts for generals
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is planning to announce further cuts to the number of generals and admirals in an address set for Wednesday.
According to Pentagon officials, Hegseth will direct all the military services to double the 10% reduction that he ordered last spring to the roughly 800 flag and general officer positions, making it a 20% total decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027.
Trump or Hegseth already have fired or pushed to retire more than two dozen military leaders since taking office, including the Army’s top uniformed officer, Gen. Randy George.
Hegseth will make the announcement in a speech to troops at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, the second year in a row he will deliver what the Pentagon is calling his “State of the Force” address.
Fox News earlier reported the new reductions.
Senate Republican blocks Democratic resolution disapproving of taxpayer-funded ads promoting Trump
New Hampshire Sen. Maggie Hassan went to the Senate floor on Tuesday and tried to pass a resolution by unanimous consent that said it is the “sense of the Senate” that the campaign-style ads promoting President Donald Trump should not be funded by taxpayers.
Political messages “should not come at the cost of hard-earned American tax dollars,” Hassan said.
Wyoming Sen. Cynthia Lummis objected, comparing the ads to government public service announcements of the past, like anti-drug campaigns and pro-vaccination messages during the coronavirus pandemic. “I don’t recall a single Democrat rushing to the floor to object to any of them,” Lummis said.
Hassan responded that “people know the difference between a PSA and a political ad.”
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said this week that he believes the ads should not be funded by taxpayers.
Trump says he’ll do a 32-day campaign tour ahead of the midterms
Despite the president’s approval ratings sinking to near historic lows ahead of Election Day in November, Trump maintained of Republican candidates around the country, “They all want me to go” and help out in their races.
He said he’d be launching a 32-day blitz to the midterm elections that would begin on Thursday with a trip to Texas.
Trump added that he’d also be going to Ohio and “all different places.”
All of Trump’s planned stops haven’t yet been made public, but he is set to visit Alabama on Friday and Nebraska on Monday.
Some top Republican elected officials and candidates have begun to distance themselves from Trump, calling for an end to the war in Iran or softening of his immigration policies. But the president believes the best way he can help the GOP is personally rallying his “Make America Great Again” base in different areas.
Trump calls Google CEO a ‘monster’ — in a good way
Trump introduced Google CEO Sundar Pichai to reporters in an unusual way.
“This guy is a monster, and nobody knows,” Trump said approvingly. Pichai described the voluntary AI agreement this way, using Trump’s new branding for artificial intelligence:
“We are signing up to a set of processes and controls like we do in other areas, like financial controls, in a company. And we are bringing those well-known best practices to the development of superintelligence,” Pichai told reporters.
The text of the new accord is not yet available. Here’s how Zuckerberg described it
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg told reporters at the White House that the new accord included “a set of principles and commitments around building robust internal controls and detecting if there are any issues with the technology.”
Zuckerberg, who had distanced his company from calls for a slowdown in AI, said the new agreement would be “coupled with multiple layers of auditing and controls, starting with internal risk review, external auditors and evaluators and agreeing that we’re going to have all of our boards of directors independently review the reports that come from the auditors.”
Trump says data centers are ‘absolutely beautiful’
The president has spent months defending tech companies building data centers around the country, even amid a growing backlash from voters on the right and the left.
He made the case again during his impromptu White House driveway question-and-answer session. But this time, Trump drew on his decades as a New York real estate developer and suggested that centers make very aesthetically pleasing buildings.
“By the way, I’m very good at real estate. Some of those buildings are absolutely beautiful,” Trump said. “They’re big and they’re, you know, big, strong, powerful buildings. But they’re beautiful and they add greatly to a community.”
Anthropic’s Amodei says AI safety mechanism still under discussion
One of the loudest voices on the risks of AI -- Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei -- said after the meeting that he thinks the industry can protect safety.
“But I think the technology has very real risks. And, you know, the mechanism, how we address those risks is still under discussion,” Amodei said during the White House driveway news conference.
Amodei had dinner with Trump on Sunday night and was part of Tuesday’s industry meeting.
Trump and AI leaders have signed a voluntary accord for reviews of artificial intelligence after White House meeting
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said that he and a large group of leaders of artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews of the technology during a meeting at the White House.
“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters outside the West Wing.
Details of the accord were not immediately available.
Supreme Court lets quick deportations to third countries resume for now while it weighs Trump policy
The high court said Tuesday it will hear arguments on whether migrants must have a chance to object.
The order lifts for now an appeals court ruling. Federal attorneys said the lower court’s decision forced the cancellation of a deportation flight carrying about 70 people.
Under a series of often-secret agreements, Trump’s Republican administration has deported some 25,000 people to more than two dozen countries. The case comes amid a sweeping immigration crackdown by the Trump administration.
Trump praises AI self-regulation and data centers at White House tech luncheon
The president called his White House lunch meeting with top tech executives to discuss artificial intelligence “very productive” and said that those gathered were united in that “we love our country and we love the world, and we want to make sure it’s a safe place.”
Trump said the tech leaders were “the greatest, most brilliant people in the world,” but offered few details on what AI guardrails might have been discussed.
Instead he praised “self-regulation,” and added “we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that.”
The president repeated his defense of data centers being built around the country – despite them becoming increasingly unpopular.
Trump said the assembled tech leaders would work to make communities getting data centers happy by supplying oil and gas, making local education donations and providing tax revenue.
“Data centers are going to be very popular,” he said, because tech leaders “want to see communities that are safe and happy.”
Trump added: “Otherwise, they’ll be forced to go overseas or other locations.”
Alaska’s GOP senator says parties are divided over energy development in the state
Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska said the war in Iran is temporary, but that a “forever war” is one Democrats wage against oil and gas projects in the state.
Sullivan is locked in a tight reelection campaign against Democrat Mary Peltola. He told The Associated Press that fuel costs are a “huge issue” and that people are hurting.
He said he’s focused on that through efforts that include supporting funding for a low-income heating assistance program and a temporary moratorium on U.S. exports of diesel until the war with Iran is over.
Many small rural communities accessible only by air or water rely on diesel for heat and electricity, with some shipments coming on barges before rivers freeze.
Sullivan spoke after a campaign rally in Juneau. He and Peltola have cast themselves as champions of oil and gas development in Alaska, even as Sullivan has tried to tie Peltola to national Democrats, who have often fought to restrict drilling.
Navy jet crashed into Atlantic Ocean after equipment failure
A fighter jet that crashed into the Atlantic Ocean while landing on the aircraft carrier USS Dwight D. Eisenhower suffered a failure to the arresting gear that was designed to bring the jet to a halt after landing.
“Two Naval aviators assigned to Carrier Air Wing 3 subsequently ejected from their aircraft following an arresting gear failure and were promptly recovered by search-and-rescue personnel,” the Navy said in a statement released Tuesday.
According to the Navy, the jet was a E/A-18G Growler that was assigned to Electronic Attack Squadron 130, also known as the “Zappers.”
Eight sailors, including the two aviators, were evaluated by medical personnel and five were flown off the ship for follow-on treatment.
Jack Smith hearing wraps up
The four-hour hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee was marked by partisan squabbling over what Republicans have characterized as political prosecutions against Trump as he sought a return to the White House.
Smith repeatedly defended the work of his investigative team, telling lawmakers: “Anybody who has worked with me or knows me during the course of my career knows that I would not let politics play a role.”
The hearing came as Republicans have pushed for Smith to himself be prosecuted. Smith said he “will not be silenced by continued threats of prosecution from the president or others.”
GAO tells lawmakers that Trump can’t withhold more than $800 million
President Donald Trump is not permitted to withhold beyond Wednesday, the end of the fiscal year, more than $800 million in spending approved by Congress.
That’s according to a review from the Government Accountability Office that was sent to federal lawmakers and Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday and obtained by The Associated Press.
The president proposed rescinding spending from 11 appropriations accounts, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.
But the GAO said federal law provides that funds proposed for rescission must be made available unless Congress completes action on a bill rescinding them.
“Any withholding of appropriated funds beyond their date of expiration, regardless of size, subverts both the constitutional process for enacting federal law and Congress’s constitutional power of the purse,” wrote the GAO’s general counsel.
US targets Iran’s military supply chain with new sanctions
The United States is targeting people and companies around the globe that it accuses of being financial facilitators or enablers of Iran’s military supply chain.
The Trump administration is pushing forward with economic warfare against Tehran at a time when renewed diplomacy between the two countries remains uncertain.
The latest action by the Treasury Department on Tuesday is part of the administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast” campaign, which is aimed at severing “critical financial lifelines” for the already heavily sanctioned Iranian government.
“Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
Ten individuals and entities based in Iran, Hong Kong and Pakistan now face sanctions over accusations of procuring weapons and weapon components for Iran’s defense ministry as it fights its now seven-month war against the U.S.
EPA union sues Zeldin over termination of labor contract
A union representing thousands of employees at the Environmental Protection Agency is suing EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin over his termination of a collective bargaining agreement with workers.
The American Federation of Government Employees Council 238 says Zeldin’s action last year unlawfully stripped about 8,000 federal workers of protections that help them do their jobs, follow sound science and speak up without fear of retaliation.
Zeldin abruptly terminated the labor contract in August 2025, two months after 139 employees signed a “declaration of dissent” with his policies, saying they “undermine the EPA mission of protecting human health and the environment.”
EPA ultimately fired 20 employees who signed the dissent letter, and suspended 119 without pay, the union says. Of those disciplined, 110 were covered by the collective bargaining agreement.
The union called Zeldin’s action an attempt to silence workers and remove protections for employees who spoke out about political interference with the agency’s scientific work.
Tech industry leaders joining Trump, Vance, top Cabinet members for White House lunch focused on AI
The president is hosting a White House lunch on artificial intelligence in the face of growing calls for the government to establish guardrails that can help contain the technology.
Attendees include Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Nikesh Arora of Palo Alto Networks, Amazon chief Jeff Bezos, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Brad Gerstner of Altimeter and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.
Also on hand will be Tesla and Space X’s Elon Musk and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.
Those industry leaders will join Trump and Vance, as well as House Speaker Mike Johnson, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
Trump to campaign in solidly red Nebraska with midterms looming
The president has repeatedly promised to travel to competitive areas around the country, even as his approval ratings sink and Republicans increasingly scramble to try and hold control of Congress after Election Day in November.
But Trump is instead holding a rally on Monday in Grand Island, in solidly red, south-central Nebraska.
The state has a competitive congressional race in Omaha, but where Trump is going is a different, GOP-held district and media market, with an election that isn’t expected to be close.
Trump’s trip could be an effort to counter Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running for Nebraska’s Senate seat against incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts.
But the president hitting Grand Island comes as the midterm map is full of Senate races in other states where Democrats have far better shots of flipping GOP seats.
GOP’s Schmitt appears to mix-up teams during Smith accusation
Republicans spent much of the Senate hearing trying to trip up Smith and impeach his credibility.
In one notable moment, Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt accused Smith of traveling to Atlanta and attending a game for the city’s NBA team — the Hawks — in February 2024 while Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis was facing scrutiny for her romantic relationship with a special prosecutor in the Georgia 2020 election case.
But it appeared Schmitt got his teams confused. Smith said he had actually been at a game that day for the University of Iowa Hawkeyes in Maryland.
America.gov changes politically thorny answers moments after launch
As it initially launched, the site’s question-and-answer function answered some political questions truthfully — noting correctly that Biden won the 2020 election and that Obama’s 2009 inaugural crowd was bigger than Trump’s in 2017.
Within moments, however, the site began modifying its answers.
After originally reporting that Biden won in 2020, it refused to answer the question subsequently, saying it didn’t answer political inquiries.
Same went for a question on crowd size at Obama’s inauguration versus Trump’s first one.
The site also offered more muddled answers on other things Trump frequently says that aren’t true — like the Strait of Hormuz being fully reopened to commercial traffic.

sources.news_title: 'The worst!' Trump silences CNN for calling him out at bizarre outdoor press conference
sources.text:
President Donald Trump shouted down a reporter he identified as being from CNN after the journalist challenged his claim that artificial intelligence companies can police themselves.
The clash came Tuesday as Trump took questions outside the White House with tech leaders standing behind him, NBC News reported. The president had just hosted a private lunch with nearly 20 tech executives, and he kept pushing back on calls for new safety rules.
The appearance came after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called earlier this month for leading firms to slow down, as companies logged mounting cases of AI agents going rogue.
"Mr. President, tell us why the world should not be concerned about AI. Why there shouldn't be guardrails?" one reporter asked Trump.
"Because we have people that love our country and love the world," Trump replied.
"It requires more than love, doesn't it, sir?" a second reporter pressed.
"No. It requires this and the smartest people in the world," Trump said. "And we had a great meeting today. Every one of them."
"Who should be held accountable when the AI agents commit a crime?" another reporter asked.
"It's not AI. It's SI," Trump answered. "…We've changed the name officially today. We've changed the name, Steve, officially to SI. OK?"
"SI, like SI, SI, instead of AI. You know what that means? Superintelligence," he continued.
"So, Mr. President, we really don't have to answer that?" a reporter asked.
"So the name… I guess that's really quite an announcement, because the name has been officially changed by the biggest, the smartest, the greatest people anywhere in the world at this," Trump said.
Later, a reporter asked Trump whether anything he heard at the lunch had changed his mind about guardrails.
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police," Trump said.
"If we do this right, we work with the president and everyone here, we can win safely," Amodei told reporters after they called him to the front of the group.
"Do you think that self-policing is enough? Are you…" another reporter asked Trump.
"Hold it! Hold it! Hold it! CNN! Fake news!" Trump shouted.
"Do you think that self-policing is enough?" the reporter tried again.
"The worst!" Trump said.
Trump announced this month that he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, and a federal judge has temporarily blocked the move, NBC News reported.
"Mark, you wanna discuss what you learned?" Trump said, turning to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg after the reporter asked for a follow-up.
"It's tremendous good. We want it to be safe. And they're gonna be watching over each other," Trump said after Zuckerberg described the accord the executives had signed.

Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI

US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival.
Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November.
The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents.
During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US was "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and did not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors.
"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China."
Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remained steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology.
"Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way".
Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hindered AI governance.
At a later White House lunch with representatives of government agencies and technology companies - including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta - Trump said among those present, there was "a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation".
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Trump said that the technology leaders had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from the potential hazards of AI.
A "Super Intelligence Czar" would likely be named in the coming days, Trump added. The president signed an executive order, external on Tuesday afternoon that will formally change the name of AI to "Super Intelligence" in government documents.
Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place.
A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity.
A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused.
The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

sources.news_title: Why Sundar Pichai, Jensen Huang and Other AI Leaders Met Trump
sources.text:
- Trump brought leading AI and technology executives to the White House.
- The companies agreed to voluntary safety controls and external audits.
- Trump also directed federal agencies to use “Super Intelligence” instead of “AI”.
Why were Sundar Pichai, Jensen Huang, Greg Brockman and Satya Nadella all in the same room with US President Donald Trump?
The answer goes beyond a meeting of technology executives. The White House gathering brought together leaders from different parts of the artificial intelligence economy as Trump sought to push the US towards faster AI development while asking the industry to take greater responsibility for managing its risks.
Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella were among the executives at the White House on Tuesday (29), alongside Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, xAI's Elon Musk and other technology leaders.
The meeting resulted in a voluntary agreement on AI safety, with companies committing to internal controls, independent external audits and board-level reviews. Trump described the agreement as “morally binding”, while the companies' own document says the measures could eventually be incorporated into laws or regulations.
Meet the people behind the AI race
The significance of the gathering becomes clearer when you look at what the executives represent.
Sundar Pichai leads Google, which develops its own frontier AI models and operates one of the world's largest technology infrastructures. His presence put one of the biggest AI research and consumer technology companies at the table.
Jensen Huang heads Nvidia, whose processors have become a crucial part of the computing infrastructure used to train and operate advanced AI models. Huang was seated immediately beside Trump during the lunch.
Greg Brockman represented OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT and one of the leading developers of frontier AI models. OpenAI has also been dealing with questions about the safety of increasingly autonomous AI systems.
Satya Nadella leads Microsoft, a major cloud computing provider and one of OpenAI's biggest commercial partners. Microsoft's Azure infrastructure provides computing capacity for advanced AI workloads.
But they were not the only major figures around the table.
Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive, represents another major AI developer building its own models and products.
Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, has been one of the more prominent voices in the technology industry warning about the risks of increasingly capable AI.
Elon Musk, who leads xAI, was also at the meeting. The seating plan showed Musk and Huang on either side of Trump, while Pichai and Zuckerberg were also seated close to the president.
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Palantir CEO Alex Karp, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and other executives also attended.
Together, the group represented much more than companies making chatbots. The wider AI industry now depends on chips, cloud computing, data centres, networking equipment, cybersecurity and enterprise software.
What did Trump want from the meeting?
Trump has repeatedly argued that the US should not slow down AI development because of regulation, particularly as Washington competes with China for technological leadership.
At the White House, he again backed rapid expansion of AI infrastructure, including data centres, while saying communities hosting those facilities should benefit financially. Reuters reported that Trump also stressed the importance of the US remaining at the forefront of AI development.
At the same time, he wants technology companies to take responsibility for policing their own systems.
The White House Accord on Super Intelligence sets out four layers of controls and audits. These include internal safety controls, reviews by independent external auditors and consideration of audit findings by company boards. The participating companies also agreed to meet regularly to develop safety standards and best practices.
The agreement is voluntary rather than a legally enforceable regulatory framework. Trump nevertheless described it as “morally binding” and said the companies understood that they needed to “self-police”.
The approach comes as the industry faces growing scrutiny over AI systems behaving in unexpected ways. OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported or faced scrutiny over incidents involving increasingly autonomous systems, while concerns have grown about cybersecurity, misuse and whether companies can adequately control their most capable models.
Nvidia's Huang said at the meeting that he saw no conflict between technological innovation and safety, according to CBS News. Other executives have taken a more cautious view of the speed at which frontier AI is developing.
Trump also said he planned to name an AI czar, according to CBS News, and discussed the possibility of a 10-person committee to oversee the industry.
Why is Trump calling it ‘Super Intelligence’?
The meeting also coincided with Trump's decision to change the language used by the US executive branch.
In an executive order signed on Tuesday, Trump directed federal agencies to use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” instead of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” in official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents and other non-statutory documents.
The order argues that today's frontier systems have capabilities beyond what was envisaged when the term artificial intelligence was first introduced.
For now, however, the order does not create an entirely new legal category of technology. It says “Super Intelligence” and “SI” will use the existing statutory definition of artificial intelligence unless a later presidential action or Act of Congress changes it. The administration has also been given 60 days to propose a federal definition of “Super Intelligence”.
That leaves the White House meeting with a clear message: Trump wants the US AI industry to build faster, invest heavily in the infrastructure behind it and take responsibility for safety without waiting for a new layer of government regulation.
And that explains why Pichai, Huang, Brockman, Nadella, Zuckerberg, Amodei, Musk and other technology leaders were sitting around the same table.

sources.news_title: Trump Promotes AI Accord with Technology Leaders, Advocates for Data Centre Development
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump announced an artificial intelligence accord on Tuesday, which was signed in conjunction with several leading technology companies. This framework aims to enhance internal safeguards amid rising concerns regarding the risks associated with powerful AI systems. Trump shared the one-page document on Truth Social, following discussions with tech executives at the White House, describing the agreement as “morally binding”.
The document includes signatures from Trump and prominent executives from Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, X, and Nvidia. The accord encourages these companies to implement multiple layers of controls for their AI systems, which encompasses independent audits, board-level oversight, and close monitoring during both training and deployment phases of their models.
As part of the agreement, firms are recommended to collaborate with external auditors to ensure that their monitoring systems are functioning as designed. Additionally, the firms should establish an independent board committee tasked with overseeing these processes and evaluating reports from internal and external auditors. The accord emphasizes internal measures to evaluate AI model capabilities, particularly concerning cybersecurity and safety threats.
Trump’s Support for Data Centres Amid Controversy
In conjunction with the AI accord, Trump reiterated his backing for the swift expansion of data centres, vital to the technology sector’s development of robust AI models. Despite rising opposition in various US communities regarding the impact of such facilities on electricity demand and local infrastructure, Trump asserted that these centres would yield financial benefits to surrounding areas.
The consumption of electricity by data centres is significant, as they provide the necessary computing power for AI operations. This rapid growth of data centres has sparked concerns among residents about potential increases in power demand and utility costs. The White House has subsequently sought strategies to ensure that the growth of these facilities will not adversely affect household electricity prices.
This developing situation has become politically sensitive, with the Trump administration advocating for the expansion of AI infrastructure while addressing concerns regarding its societal impacts. As technology firms collaborated with the administration, discussions focused on how to foster community acceptance for new data centres.
Growing Concerns Regarding AI Systems
The unveiling of the accord occurs amidst heightened scrutiny surrounding advanced AI applications following several incidents reported by firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic. These companies have detailed instances where their AI agents operated outside their intended parameters, raising alarms about the unintended actions of increasingly autonomous models.
The White House meeting convened several influential industry leaders, including Greg Brockman from OpenAI, Dario Amodei from Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg from Meta, Sundar Pichai from Google, and Jensen Huang from Nvidia. Zuckerberg stated that all firms involved had collectively agreed to create strong internal controls for their AI systems, with routine assessments by auditors to ensure compliance and effectiveness.
Additionally, Trump indicated he is contemplating the establishment of a ten-member panel to oversee AI safety, although he did not disclose potential members of this group. This move is part of a broader push by his administration for accelerated AI development and infrastructure growth. Earlier in June, Trump signed a directive aimed at advancing AI adoption within the US national security framework, highlighting the importance of accountability and release of appropriate safeguards.
On a related note, Trump expressed his reluctance to engage in cooperative efforts with Chinese President Xi Jinping concerning AI governance, suggesting that collaboration might weaken the competitive edge of American firms. However, during Xi’s recent visit to Washington, both the US and China agreed to establish a dialogue on the potential risks and advantages associated with “super intelligence” and to create a communication channel for AI-related incidents.

sources.news_title: Trump Signs A “Morally Binding” Agreement With Tech Leaders To Promote Safer AI Development
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he had signed a “morally binding” agreement with major technology companies to promote safer artificial intelligence development, as concerns over increasingly autonomous AI systems intensify and the White House continues to resist calls for tougher federal regulation.
Speaking after a White House luncheon with some of the biggest names in the technology industry, Trump said he was seeing “tremendous self-policing” across the sector and said his administration was considering a committee of about 10 people to oversee the AI industry.
House Speaker Mike Johnson described the agreement as a voluntary statement of principles for the industry, with the White House expected to provide guidance on AI development. The text of the agreement had not been publicly released as of Tuesday.

The arrangement places the administration’s preferred approach, industry-led oversight rather than broad federal restrictions, directly against a growing push from some AI researchers and executives for stronger safeguards as systems become more capable of acting autonomously.
Trump said earlier Tuesday that the government would not halt AI development and argued that existing government institutions, including the Justice Department and FBI, already provide a layer of oversight.
“There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that,” Trump said. “But the self-regulation is very important.”
The White House’s position comes at a particularly consequential moment for the industry. OpenAI has just postponed the release of its GPT-6.1 Astra model after internal testing found that the system did not meet the company’s safety and alignment standards. OpenAI said the model had problems staying within scope and authorization and accurately communicating what work it had performed.
The agreement arrives as the debate over the pace of AI development has moved from theoretical concerns to problems involving systems capable of taking actions with limited human intervention.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has repeatedly warned about risks associated with increasingly capable AI, said outside the White House that rules addressing those risks were still being discussed.
“We all need to work together to make sure that we can win, and we can win safely,” Amodei said. “If we do this right, if we work with the president and everyone here, we can win safely.”
Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have both joined calls for greater caution around the development of frontier AI, putting them at times at odds with other technology executives and with Trump’s emphasis on maintaining America’s lead in the technology.
The immediate disagreement is less about whether AI should be made safer than about who should establish the rules and how binding those rules should be.
Trump’s approach places considerable responsibility on companies themselves. Johnson’s description of the White House agreement as voluntary reinforces that distinction.
The challenge is that the capabilities being discussed are becoming increasingly difficult to separate from questions of public safety and national security. OpenAI’s decision to hold back GPT-6.1 Astra illustrates the problem: the company determined through its own internal testing that the model was not yet sufficiently reliable in following authorization boundaries and reporting its actions.
That decision came after OpenAI had already described Astra as a highly capable system requiring stronger safeguards. Earlier in September, the company said it had delayed parts of Astra’s development and release while testing protections against cyber misuse and unauthorized actions.
The developments give the voluntary agreement an immediate test. If frontier companies are increasingly identifying serious problems through internal evaluations, the question becomes whether voluntary commitments can provide consistent standards across companies and whether those commitments can be independently verified.
Tech Industry Gathers Around Trump
The White House luncheon brought together an unusually large concentration of technology executives.
A seating chart posted by Trump showed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk seated beside the president, with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Google’s Sundar Pichai also nearby.
Vice President JD Vance sat opposite Trump between Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Johnson. Other attendees included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Amodei, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, and senior administration officials including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
The gathering also came as OpenAI hosted its annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco, creating an unusual contrast between the administration’s discussion of AI safety in Washington and one of the industry’s major product and developer events on the same day.
AMD CEO Lisa Su said she was “very encouraged” by the White House event and described the atmosphere as marked by “a lot of optimism and a sense of responsibility.”
“I mean, at the end of the day, it’s our responsibility to show the power of the technology as well as ensure that it’s very safe,” Su said.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp similarly emphasized corporate responsibility, saying ahead of the event that companies need to address known dangers and that Americans should not be subject to different standards simply because the technology is being developed by the private sector.
“The main issue that you have and I have is we have to take responsibility for the dangers we’re aware of,” Karp said. “All of us do. And by the way, American people don’t want separate rules for tech people and for themselves.”
That tension is likely to remain central to the debate. Technology companies have substantial incentives to develop and commercialize increasingly capable systems, while the same companies are being asked to determine when those systems are sufficiently safe to deploy.
Trump Links AI Safety to U.S. Competitiveness
Trump’s position is also closely tied to his broader emphasis on maintaining U.S. leadership in AI.
He described the technology’s leading developers as “the most brilliant people in the world” and said the United States has “a very big lead” that he intends to preserve.
The administration has continued promoting rapid AI deployment, including the construction of large data centers that have generated local opposition over energy use and other impacts. Trump described the data centers as “a very positive thing” and said technology companies want communities around them to be safe and prosperous.
He also said he planned to name a new AI czar within three to four days.
The administration’s emphasis on competitiveness creates a major constraint on any attempt to slow AI development. Stronger safety requirements could increase development costs or delay the deployment of frontier systems, while the White House has repeatedly argued that the United States cannot afford to surrender its technological advantage.
That tension is escalating significantly because China is simultaneously investing heavily in AI infrastructure and domestic models.
The White House now faces two objectives that can pull in different directions: encouraging companies to move quickly enough to maintain U.S. technological leadership while ensuring that autonomous systems do not create risks that companies cannot adequately manage themselves.
The voluntary agreement announced Tuesday represents an attempt to reconcile those objectives without imposing a broad new regulatory framework.

sources.news_title: Trump and AI leaders agree on voluntary safety standards for technology
sources.text:
Get you up to speed: Trump and major AI executives sign “morally binding” voluntary controls: “It’s almost like a constitution”
President Trump and leaders of major artificial intelligence companies signed voluntary safety standards during a meeting at the White House. The accord includes commitments to establish internal controls and audits for AI technology while discussions were held about forming a committee to oversee AI development.
The tech companies agreed to implement four layers of controls and audits to ensure the effectiveness of their AI models, which include internal evaluations, external firm audits, and board reviews. President Trump plans to announce an “AI czar” within the next three or four days to oversee the sector.
President Trump announced plans to appoint an “AI czar” within the next few days and indicated the formation of a 10-person committee to oversee AI developments. In response to concerns from politicians like Democratic Senator Mark Warner, who called for mandatory regulations, the administration maintains that voluntary safety standards and self-regulation by tech firms are sufficient for managing risks associated with advanced AI technology.
What remains unclear — It is still unknown how the proposed 10-person committee and the “AI czar” will function and be selected.
Trump and AI leaders agree on voluntary safety standards for technology
President Trump and the leaders of the country’s largest artificial intelligence companies have signed a set of voluntary safety standards, as calls mount for tighter guardrails on AI technology.
“It’s almost like a constitution, in a way,” Mr. Trump said while flanked by SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, Google’s Sundar Pichai and a throng of other tech executives.
Following a lunch meeting at the White House, Johnson said the group signed an accord on “super intelligence” — Mr. Trump’s preferred term for AI. He described it as a “joint commitment” and “statement of principles” that will voluntarily hold the companies to “robust internal controls.”
Asked if the deal was binding, Mr. Trump said: “I think it’s morally binding.”
“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” the president later said.
The tech companies committed to “four layers of controls and audits” to ensure the AI models are acting as intended, including internal evaluations, audits by an external firm and reviews by each company’s board of directors, according to a copy of the one-page accord that Mr. Trump posted to Truth Social. They also agreed to “meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems.”
“Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations,” said the accord. “Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this.”
Mr. Trump said the AI leaders also discussed forming a 10-person committee to “watch over the enterprise.” And the president said he plans to name an “AI czar” in the next three or four days.
Also on Tuesday, the president signed an executive order directing the federal government to use the term “Super Intelligence” instead of artificial intelligence.
The rare meeting between competing tech titans followed months of growing concern from researchers, politicians and industry figures that ever-more-powerful AI technology could pose safety risks.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported instances of their AI models going rogue and gaining unauthorized access to other companies’ systems, or being used for dangerous purposes. And Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both companies, publicly warned earlier this month that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” He argued AI systems could gain sweeping power over the physical world and become capable of improving themselves without human input.
Some industry leaders, including executives at Anthropic and OpenAI, have called for a slowdown in AI development to better manage the risk. But other figures, like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, have argued some of the warnings are overblown.
Huang said Tuesday that “there’s no conflict between innovation, technology and safety,” arguing that tech companies are developing stronger AI safety technology as they improve AI’s capabilities.
Mr. Trump has not backed stricter AI regulations, instead favoring voluntary safety reviews. He has frequently warned that a nationwide AI slowdown could dent the country’s economy and give China’s tech industry a chance to catch up.
The president told reporters Tuesday that AI will lead to “unbelievable growth for our country,” and if bad actors seek to exploit it, “we’re going to be able to nab them.” He also said tech companies have an incentive to police themselves and each other because “their companies are at stake.”
Beyond the safety worries, there are also mounting concerns about the impact that AI could have on the world — from the potential for large-scale job loss to the rapid development of data centers to support advanced AI models.
As more state and local governments push back on data center development, Mr. Trump said communities that accept the facilities will “greatly benefit financially.”
“The data centers are making an absolute fortune. But now, the people are going to benefit directly, whether it’s teachers that get paid a bonus, whether it’s people that live in the community that get paid a dividend,” he told WTX US News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes.
But lawmakers who favor more stringent AI regulations may be skeptical of voluntary standards set by the industry. In a statement shortly after Tuesday’s meeting, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia called for Congress to pass mandatory testing, evaluation and incident reporting rules for the most advanced AI models.
“The companies building the most powerful AI systems are warning us that the technology is advancing faster than our safeguards,” Warner said. “The president’s response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves.”
